pages.body:
What should you do when the text you have is not the text you need? The paper opens on that mismatch: unlabelled text exists in enormous quantity, while the labelled examples for any single language understanding task are few and expensive to produce.

### The imbalance, and why it bites

[[natural-language-understanding]] is not one task in this paper. It is an umbrella over a set of supervised problems — textual entailment, question answering, [[semantic-similarity]], document classification — that share an input type and little else. Each comes with its own dataset, its own labels, its own notion of a correct answer. [[table-1]] lays out the twelve datasets the paper will eventually use.

Grouping them under one name is what makes a single-model claim sayable at all. If these are separate problems, one model per problem is the natural answer.

Inside that group sits the actual constraint, [[labeled-data-scarcity]]. The annotated sets are small: [[rte]], one of the twelve, has 2,490 training examples. Annotation is slow and costly, so the small ones stay small.

Scarcity hurts a particular kind of model hardest. A discriminatively trained network learns $P(y \mid x)$, so its only teacher is the label attached to each input; with 2,490 labels there are 2,490 supervision events. A generative model predicts the data itself, so every token in a corpus is a supervision event. That contrast is [[generative-vs-discriminative-training]], and it is why unlabelled text looks like an unused resource rather than a different problem.

The paper grants that this is already established at the word level. [[word-embedding-transfer|Pre-trained word embeddings]] are named as the most compelling existing evidence that unlabelled text helps supervised tasks. The open ground is everything above the word.

### The two things nobody had settled

Moving beyond word-level information was hard for two reasons, and the introduction states them as two questions rather than two difficulties.

The first is [[choice-of-pretraining-objective]]. Language modelling, machine translation and discourse coherence had all been tried as unsupervised objectives, and each came out ahead on some tasks and behind on others. There was no ordering to appeal to.

The second is [[how-to-transfer-representations]]. Even granting a good pre-trained representation, prior work moved it into a target task by some mixture of task-specific architecture changes, staged learning schedules, and extra auxiliary losses. No single recipe was standard.

These two questions are not independent of the scarcity problem — they are what stands between the abundance of raw text and the shortage of labels. That is the sense in which the paper's [[two-stage-training-procedure|two-stage recipe]] presupposes scarcity: without it there would be no reason to pay for a pre-training stage at all.

### What the rest of the paper is doing

Every later choice answers one of the two. [[language-modeling-objective|The language modelling loss $L_1$]] is the answer to the first question, chosen rather than derived. [[supervised-fine-tuning]] with [[task-specific-input-transformations|input transformations]] is the answer to the second: keep the architecture fixed and reshape the task input instead. Together they support the claim of a [[task-agnostic-model]].

The scarcity framing is also testable, and the paper tests it. [[ablation-no-pretraining|Removing pre-training entirely]] costs 14.8% across the tasks in [[table-5]], which is the largest of the three ablations.

Read on with one question in hand for each design decision that follows: is this answering *which objective*, or *how to transfer*? The immediate next step is where the paper places itself among existing [[semi-supervised-learning-for-nlp|semi-supervised methods]], and which of them it says it is closest to.

Using unlabelled text to help a supervised task was not new when this paper was written. So the related work section has one job: name the family the method belongs to, cut it into branches, and say which branch it joins and which it argues against.

The family is [[semi-supervised-learning-for-nlp]]: a large unlabelled corpus plus a small labelled dataset. The earliest members computed word- and phrase-level counts from raw text and passed them to a supervised model as features.

The best-known member is [[word-embedding-transfer]]. Train one vector per word on unlabelled text, then reuse that table inside a task model. The paper grants this works, and then names its ceiling: what moves across is word-level information, and the paper wants higher-level semantics.

[[phrase-and-sentence-embeddings]] is the direct response to that ceiling — learn a vector for a whole phrase or sentence instead of a word. The pattern is still the same, though. Something fixed is handed to a task model that is otherwise trained from scratch.

### Two branches, split by what the unlabelled data changes

At this point the section splits the field on a single question: what does unlabelled data get to touch?

[[unsupervised-pretraining]] lets it choose only where the weights start. The supervised objective is left exactly as it was. [[auxiliary-training-objectives]] does the reverse: initialization stays ordinary, and a second unsupervised loss is added alongside the supervised one, so the model keeps learning from raw text while it learns the task.

The paper's recipe sits in the first branch and then borrows from the second — it keeps a language modelling loss running during fine-tuning, weighted by $\lambda$ ([[eq-combined-objective]]). The two branches are presented as alternatives, but the paper takes from both.

Initialization is worth arguing about at all because of [[pretraining-as-regularization]]: the cited finding that pre-training does not merely make optimization easier, it lands the network somewhere that generalizes better.

### Inside the pre-training branch, two ways to spend the weights

Once you have a pre-trained network, you still have to decide what to do with it.

[[feature-based-transfer]] freezes it. Its hidden states become extra input features for a separate model that was designed around the target task. [[elmo-deep-contextualized-word-representations|ELMo]] is the best-known instance, and several of the baselines the paper measures against are task-built biLSTMs using exactly those features ([[table-2]], [[table-4]]).

The paper's objection is a count, not a score: [[per-task-parameter-cost]]. Every new task brings a substantial block of freshly initialized parameters, because the task model itself is new. That is the number [[minimal-extra-parameters|the paper's own transfer step]] is set up to contrast with.

The other way is [[lm-pretraining-then-finetuning-predecessors]], which the paper calls the closest line to its own: pre-train with a language modelling objective, then fine-tune the whole network. [[semi-supervised-sequence-learning]] and [[ulmfit]] both do this for [[text-classification]].

Here the paper agrees with the shape and disagrees about the network. Its argument is [[lstm-short-range-limitation]]: recurrent pre-trained models keep their predictions local, so less structure survives the transfer. This is stated as a reason for a design choice, and the supporting evidence is indirect — the zero-shot curves in [[fig-2]] rise more smoothly for the transformer than for an LSTM, which is not a direct measurement of dependency length.

You should now be able to read [[two-stage-training-procedure]] and say, for each piece of it, which prior branch it keeps and which one it is answering.

Raw text is everywhere; labelled examples for any one language understanding task are few and expensive ([[labeled-data-scarcity]]). So what is the least you can change about ordinary supervised training to make all that unlabelled text count?

The paper's answer is that the raw text should decide *where supervised training starts*, not what it optimizes. That is the [[two-stage-training-procedure]], and everything else in the paper is a consequence of taking it seriously.

### The same weights, used twice

Stage one fits a network to predict the next token over a large unlabelled corpus ([[generative-pretraining]]). Stage two takes those finished parameters and continues training them on a target task's labelled data with that task's own loss ([[supervised-fine-tuning]]).

The load-bearing word is *initial*. The pre-trained weights are a starting point, and from there they keep moving under the supervised gradient.

That is what [[transfer-learning]] means here, and it is a specific choice rather than the obvious one. The alternative on offer at the time was [[feature-based-transfer]]: freeze the pre-trained model, read out its hidden states, and feed them as extra inputs to a separate network built for the task. Under that arrangement the task network's parameters are all freshly initialized, so the transferred model helps only as a feature extractor.

Fine-tuning the whole stack instead means the new parameters per task are close to none. Placing the recipe this way puts it inside [[semi-supervised-learning-for-nlp]] — unlabelled data changing the initialization rather than the objective.

One more assumption rides along. The introduction states the target tasks need not come from the same domain as the unlabelled corpus ([[domain-mismatch-tolerance]]). The paper asserts this rather than testing it directly; what stands behind it is that twelve datasets, none of them books, are all fine-tuned from one book-trained model.

### One stack, not twelve

If nothing is frozen and nothing substantial is added, the network you fine-tune is the network you pre-trained. That is the [[task-agnostic-model]] claim: one architecture, pre-trained once, applied to every task without redesign. The stack in question is a [[multi-layer-transformer-decoder]].

The contrast is with [[task-specific-architectures]], the prevailing practice of hand-designing a network around each task's structure. The paper's objection is not that such networks perform badly. It is that their custom components start from scratch, so the transferred representation never reaches them.

Something still has to absorb the fact that entailment takes a sentence pair and question answering takes a document, a question and a list of candidates. The paper moves that work out of the architecture and into the input format, via [[task-specific-input-transformations]] — [[structured-inputs]] walked into one token sequence with special tokens marking the seams. [[fig-1]] draws both halves of that split: one repeated block on the left, four input shapes on the right.

### What the evidence carries

The ablation in [[table-5]] is the sharpest support for stage one: the same transformer trained directly on the supervised tasks, with no pre-training, loses 14.8 points on average. The one-model claim rests on the scoreboards — [[table-2]], [[table-3]] and [[table-4]] — which give new best published results on nine of twelve datasets.

They also record where it does not win. RTE, SST-2 and [[mrpc]] go to specialist systems, and the smallest datasets are where the general model looks weakest.

From here you can read either stage on its own terms and know what it is for: what stage one's objective is and why the corpus was chosen, then how stage two adds almost nothing to the network. The question worth carrying into both is which parts of the recipe the ablations actually isolate.

Stage one has no labels, so the first question is what to train on at all. The paper takes the signal that raw text already carries: given the tokens so far, predict the one that comes next. What [[generative-pretraining|stage one]] keeps at the end is not those predictions but the weights that learned to make them.

That signal is written as [[language-modeling-objective|$L_1$]], set out in [[eq-lm-objective]]. Over an unlabelled corpus, sum the log-probability the network gives each token conditioned on the $k$ tokens immediately before it, and move the parameters $\Theta$ to make that sum larger. This is ordinary [[maximum-likelihood-training]], with one term per token position and nothing task-specific anywhere in it.

The size of $k$ is where the objective starts making demands. Here it is [[context-window-512-tokens|512 tokens]], which is long enough that a prediction can reach back past the current sentence. That reach is the point: the paper wants the model to pick up [[long-range-dependencies-gpt1|long-range dependencies]], the pronoun whose antecedent sat three sentences earlier, or the passage detail that answers a question asked later. The corpus was chosen to supply them, which is the argument made on the [[bookscorpus]] page.

### What the loss forces the architecture to be

$L_1$ is scored at every position of a sequence at once, so one forward pass over 512 tokens has to produce 512 separate predictions. That only works if no position can see its own answer. [[masked-self-attention]] enforces it: a position attends to itself and to earlier positions, never to later ones. Drop the mask and the objective becomes copying rather than prediction.

Masking is also why the encoder is not needed. There is no source sequence to read, only the model's own past, so the paper keeps a [[decoder-only-stack]] and discards the other half of the original encoder-decoder design. The result is the [[multi-layer-transformer-decoder]], and [[eq-decoder-stack]] writes it out in three lines.

Line one is [[input-representation-h0|$h_0 = UW_e + W_p$]]. Attention sees an unordered set of vectors, so order has to be added at the input. [[token-embedding-matrix|$W_e$]] supplies the token vectors and [[learned-position-embeddings|$W_p$]] adds one trained vector per slot, in place of the original transformer's fixed sinusoids. A trained table has a fixed number of rows, which is why 512 is a shape in the parameters rather than a knob you can turn at test time.

Line three closes the loop: [[output-softmax-tied-embeddings|$P(u) = \mathrm{softmax}(h_n W_e^T)$]]. No separate output projection is introduced. The same embedding table is read forwards on the way in and backwards on the way out.

### The sizes actually trained

[[model-specification|The trained model]] fills in every slot the architecture leaves open. It is [[twelve-layer-depth|twelve blocks]] deep with [[hidden-state-dimension-768|768-dimensional states]]. The [[twelve-attention-heads|twelve heads]] do not each get 768 dimensions; they divide it, so 768 over 12 leaves each head a 64-dimensional subspace. The feed-forward sublayer widens 768 to [[position-wise-feedforward-3072|3072]] and projects back, a four-fold expansion. [[gelu|GELU]] replaces ReLU, [[layer-normalization-gpt1|layernorm]] runs throughout, and the paper says layernorm is why plain [[weight-initialization|$\mathcal{N}(0, 0.02)$]] initialization was enough.

The architecture choice is not free-floating. [[table-5]] reports that swapping the transformer for an LSTM inside the same framework costs 5.6 average points.

What does all this prediction leave behind? The conclusion claims [[world-knowledge|world knowledge]] and an ability to handle long-range structure. That claim is inferred rather than measured directly, from downstream gains and from the zero-shot curves in [[fig-2]], so read it as the paper's interpretation.

You can now ask the sharper question the next stage answers: these weights were fitted to predict text, so what has to change for them to predict a label instead? That is [[supervised-fine-tuning]].

The pre-training objective [[eq-lm-objective]] says what to maximize. It does not say what text to maximize it over, how that text becomes tokens, or what optimizer turns the sum into a fitted model. This chapter covers those three choices, in that order.

### Why these books

The corpus is [[bookscorpus]], over 7,000 unpublished books across genres. The reason the paper gives is not size. It is [[long-range-contiguous-text]]: sentences and paragraphs are kept in the order the author wrote them.

That property is load-bearing because of the window. A prediction conditions on the [[context-window-512-tokens]] before it. If the text a few hundred tokens back has nothing to do with the current token, the cheapest way to lower the loss is to ignore it and model the current sentence only.

Contiguous text is what gives the gradient a reason to reach further back. This is the corpus being picked for [[long-range-dependencies-gpt1]] rather than for volume.

The paper makes the point by contrast. It names [[one-billion-word-benchmark]], the corpus ELMo pre-trains on, as roughly the same size but shuffled at the sentence level, which it says destroys long-range structure. Worth being plain here: this is an argument about the data, not an experiment. The paper does not pre-train on both corpora and compare.

### From raw text to subword units

The [[text-preprocessing-pipeline]] is three steps. [[ftfy]] repairs mangled characters and standardizes some punctuation and whitespace. [[spacy-tokenizer]] splits the cleaned text into words. Then [[byte-pair-encoding-gpt1]] cuts those words into subword units.

BPE builds its vocabulary by counting. Start with characters, find the adjacent pair that occurs most often across the corpus, and fuse it into one symbol. Repeat, each merge adding one entry to the vocabulary.

Run it [[bpe-merges-40000|40,000 times]] and frequent words have been merged all the way back into single symbols, while a rare proper noun from one book stays in pieces. Nothing is out of vocabulary, because the character level is always underneath. The merge count is the one knob: fewer merges means smaller vocabulary and longer token sequences, more merges the reverse.

### Fitting the model

The [[pre-training-optimization]] settings are conventional and interlock. [[adam-optimizer-gpt1]] runs at a maximum learning rate of 2.5e-4, but training does not start there. [[linear-warmup]] raises the rate from zero across the first 2000 updates, so the steps stay small while Adam's per-parameter moment estimates are still built from very few gradients. [[cosine-annealing]] then brings the rate back down to zero over the rest of the run.

"The rest of the run" has to be a known quantity for a cosine to be defined over it, which is what [[pretraining-schedule]] fixes: 100 passes over the corpus, minibatches of 64 contiguous 512-token sequences.

The [[regularization-setup]] has the same dependence. [[residual-embedding-attention-dropout]] is ordinary. [[decoupled-weight-decay]] is chosen because of the optimizer: L2 added into the loss becomes a gradient term that Adam then rescales per parameter, so weights with small gradient history get pulled toward zero harder than weights with large history. The modified version applies the decay outside that rescaling, at $w = 0.01$, on everything except biases and gains.

The reported outcome is a [[token-level-perplexity]] of 18.4. Perplexity is the exponentiated mean negative log-likelihood per token, so 18.4 says the model is about as uncertain as a uniform choice among eighteen options. It is measured on the training corpus, under this tokenization, so it does not compare to perplexities quoted elsewhere. The paper offers it as evidence that stage one fit the data, not as a result about any task.

From here you can ask which of these choices the paper actually tests. [[fig-2]] probes the model rather than the recipe, and the settings themselves reappear almost unchanged in [[fine-tuning-hyperparameters]].

Stage one produced a stack of weights that predicts the next token. Stage two asks how to turn those weights into something that predicts a label — and how to do that the same way for every task, rather than once per task.

[[supervised-fine-tuning|Fine-tuning]] assumes a [[labeled-dataset-c|labelled dataset $C$]]: token sequences, each paired with one label. A sequence is pushed through the [[generative-pretraining|pre-trained]] stack exactly as a pre-training sequence would be. What changes is what gets read off the top.

The paper takes [[final-token-activation|the final block's activation at the last input token]] — one vector — and uses nothing else from the sequence. That collapse is what lets the classifier stay small. [[linear-output-layer-wy|One added matrix $W_y$]] multiplies the vector, and a softmax turns the product into a distribution over the task's labels; [[eq-task-head]] is the entire head. Had the head needed to read every position, it could not have been a single matrix.

Training it maximizes [[supervised-objective-l2|$L_2$]], the summed log-probability of the correct labels over $C$ ([[eq-supervised-objective]]). That is ordinary maximum-likelihood classification. The only thing separating one task from another is which $C$ you plug in.

### The language modelling loss stays on

The paper does not drop $L_1$ when fine-tuning starts. It keeps [[auxiliary-lm-objective|optimizing it alongside the label loss]], computed on the task's own labelled text rather than the pre-training corpus, giving $L_3(C) = L_2(C) + \lambda L_1(C)$ ([[eq-combined-objective]]). [[auxiliary-objective-weight|$\lambda$ is set to 0.5]].

So gradient capacity is split between predicting labels and predicting the next token, and 0.5 is the paper's chosen balance between the two pulls. The reasons given are better generalization and faster convergence.

The paper's own [[ablation-no-auxiliary-objective|ablation]] qualifies that later. Dropping the auxiliary loss actually gains 0.3 points on average ([[table-5]]); keeping it helps on the larger datasets and hurts on the smaller ones. The claim in Section 3.2 is broader than the evidence in Section 5.

### Structured inputs get flattened, not architected

Several tasks do not hand you one run of text. [[structured-inputs|Some inputs have parts]] — an ordered sentence pair, or a document with a question and candidate answers. The pre-trained model only ever saw contiguous text.

The available repair was a [[task-specific-architectures|task-specific architecture]] stacked on the transferred representation. The paper rejects it because every such module is freshly initialized and gets no transfer, which drives up [[per-task-parameter-cost|per-task parameter cost]].

It uses a [[traversal-style-approach|traversal-style approach]] instead: walk the parts of the structure into one ordered sequence. Every transformed input is bracketed by [[start-and-end-tokens|randomly initialized start and end tokens]], so the last position — the one the head reads — is the same kind of thing in every example. A [[delimiter-token|`$` delimiter]] marks where one part ends and the next begins.

[[entailment-input-transformation|Entailment]] is the plain case: premise, delimiter, hypothesis. [[similarity-input-transformation|Similarity]] needs a fix, because its two sentences have no inherent order while the readout sits at the end and so favours whichever came second; both orderings are built, run separately, and their final activations added element-wise. [[qa-and-commonsense-input-transformation|Question answering]] builds one sequence per candidate answer and softmaxes the resulting scores across candidates. [[fig-1]] draws all four shapes.

The payoff is [[minimal-extra-parameters|the parameter count the paper claims]]: $W_y$ plus delimiter embeddings, and nothing more. [[task-agnostic-model|One architecture for every task]] and [[task-specific-input-transformations|rewriting the input]] are a package deal — neither works without the other.

### What was actually run

[[fine-tuning-hyperparameters|The settings]] are the pre-training settings with four exceptions: [[fine-tuning-lr-and-batch|learning rate 6.25e-5 at batch size 32]], about four times below pre-training's peak, [[fine-tuning-lr-schedule|linear decay after a 0.2% warmup]], [[classifier-dropout|dropout 0.1 on the classifier]], and [[three-epochs-fine-tuning|three epochs]].

Three passes is a small number, and the paper offers it as something it observed rather than something it tuned.

You should now be able to read any of the twelve dataset results and say which input shape it used and which parameters were new.

The recipe makes one bet: pre-train a single stack once, then adapt it to a task by [[theme-stage-two-fine-tuning-and-input-shapes|rewriting that task's input]] instead of redesigning the network. The twelve datasets are where that bet gets settled.

First the terms of the comparison, because they shape everything after. Gains are reported as [[absolute-improvement|absolute improvements]], meaning differences in percentage points against the previous best published number rather than reductions in error. What is being beaten are [[baseline-comparisons|task-built systems]]: mostly bidirectional [[lstm-gpt1|LSTM]] architectures, some with attention or ELMo features, several of them ensembles. A few of the tasks arrive bundled through the [[glue-benchmark|GLUE benchmark]]. [[table-1]] is the full menu of [[evaluation-task-families|four families and twelve datasets]].

### Walking the four families

[[natural-language-inference|Natural language inference]] is the largest family, at five datasets. The task is to read a premise and a hypothesis, then decide whether the first entails the second, contradicts it, or leaves it open. Deciding that requires resolving [[coreference|coreference]] and handling lexical and syntactic ambiguity — the kind of structure a model would have to bring with it rather than learn from a few thousand labels.

The five are picked for different sources: image captions in [[snli|SNLI]], mixed genres in [[multinli|MultiNLI]], Wikipedia in [[qnli|QNLI]], science exams in [[scitail|SciTail]], news in [[rte|RTE]]. [[table-2]] puts the model ahead on four of them, by 5.8 points on QNLI, 5 on SciTail, 1.5 on MNLI and 0.6 on SNLI.

RTE is the exception, and it is also the smallest, at 2490 training examples against SNLI's roughly 550k. There the model gets 56.0 against 61.7 from a multi-task biLSTM. The paper suggests multi-task training would probably help, given how the larger NLI sets went, and says plainly it has not tried it.

[[question-answering-and-commonsense-reasoning|Question answering and commonsense reasoning]] is where the long pre-training context should pay off. [[race-dataset|RACE]] is exam passages with questions, chosen over [[cnn-and-squad-contrast|CNN and SQuAD]] because it has been shown to hold more reasoning-type questions than those; that contrast is the whole reason RACE is in the paper. [[story-cloze-test|Story Cloze]] asks for the right ending to a multi-sentence story. [[table-3]] holds the two largest margins in the paper, 8.9 points on Story Cloze and 5.7 on RACE, both over ensembles.

[[semantic-similarity|Semantic similarity]] asks whether two sentences mean the same thing. The model gains 4.2 points on [[qqp|QQP]] and one point on [[sts-b|STS-B]], and stays below a specialist system on [[mrpc|MRPC]].

Set STS-B beside RTE for a moment. STS-B has about 5.7k training examples, RTE 2490. One gains and one loses, so size alone does not predict where fine-tuning lands.

[[text-classification|Text classification]] is two single-sentence tasks that also disagree. [[cola|CoLA]] rises to 45.4 from a previous best of 35.0, which the paper reads as linguistic bias picked up during pre-training. [[sst-2|SST-2]] reaches 91.3% and only matches the state of the art. [[table-4]] carries both, plus the GLUE total moving from 68.9 to 72.8.

### What the count amounts to

[[state-of-the-art-9-of-12|Nine of twelve]], with RTE, MRPC and SST-2 the three that fall short. The paper reads the spread as evidence the approach works across dataset sizes, from STS-B up to SNLI. That reading holds better across families than inside NLI, where the smallest set is the one loss.

None of this says why. It establishes only that one pre-trained stack, plus a linear layer and some delimiter tokens ([[fig-1]]), covers all four input shapes. [[theme-taking-the-recipe-apart|The analysis next]] splits the credit between pre-training, the architecture and the auxiliary loss. Carry MRPC into it: that is the single dataset where swapping in an LSTM beats the transformer.

The results say the recipe works. They do not say which part of it is doing the work — the pre-training, the architecture, the extra loss during fine-tuning, or the depth of the stack. Section 5 attacks that question three ways: turn one dial, look inside the pre-trained model before fine-tuning, and remove pieces one at a time.

### Turning the depth dial

The first diagnostic is [[layers-transferred]]. Fine-tuning normally starts from all twelve pre-trained blocks. Here the paper varies how many of them are carried over, and initializes the rest fresh.

Accuracy on MultiNLI and RACE rises steadily as more layers come across — [[fig-2]], left panel — reaching about 9% for full transfer on MultiNLI over transferring embeddings alone.

The shape of that curve is the finding. It does not flatten after two or three layers, so no single layer holds the transferable content. Each block is carrying something the target task can use.

That raises the obvious follow-up. If every layer holds useful function, what function is it?

### Looking at the model before fine-tuning

[[zero-shot-behaviors]] is the attempt to answer that directly, by making the pre-trained model do the evaluation tasks with no supervised training at all.

There is an obstacle. A language model emits a distribution over next tokens; it does not emit labels. Something has to convert one into the other.

That something is [[average-token-log-probability-scoring]]: score a candidate string by the mean log-probability the model assigns its tokens. Three of the four heuristics are that one device pointed at different text. [[cola-zero-shot-heuristic|CoLA]] scores the sentence and thresholds. [[race-zero-shot-heuristic|RACE]] conditions on document and question, then takes the highest-scoring answer. [[dprd-winograd-heuristic|DPRD]] substitutes each candidate referent for the pronoun and scores the rest of the sentence. Only [[sst2-zero-shot-heuristic|SST-2]] works differently, appending the token *very* and restricting the output distribution to *positive* and *negative*.

These scores are low in absolute terms, and the heuristics are hand-designed, so the interesting quantity is not the level but the trend. In [[fig-2]]'s right panel all four climb steadily across pre-training. The paper reads that as the generative objective picking up task-relevant behaviour on its way to better next-token prediction.

The same plot carries a weaker claim. An LSTM trained the same way shows higher variance in its zero-shot scores, and the paper offers [[transformer-inductive-bias|structured attentional memory]] as the explanation. It words this as a hypothesis, and one qualitative comparison is all that stands behind it.

### Removing pieces

[[ablation-studies]] are blunter, and the numbers are in [[table-5]].

[[ablation-no-pretraining]] trains the same transformer straight on the supervised tasks. It loses 14.8% across the board — the cost of removing [[generative-pretraining]] entirely.

[[ablation-lstm-substitution]] keeps the pre-training and swaps the [[multi-layer-transformer-decoder]] for a single-layer 2048-unit LSTM. That costs 5.6 average points, and the LSTM wins on only one dataset, [[mrpc]].

Set the two side by side: 14.8 against 5.6, roughly a factor of three. Within this framework, the pre-training matters more than the architecture choice.

[[ablation-no-auxiliary-objective]] does not fit that pattern. Dropping [[auxiliary-lm-objective|the auxiliary loss]] gains 0.3 on average; it helps on the larger datasets and hurts on the smaller ones. That makes it a setting to tune per dataset, not a load-bearing part of the recipe.

You should now be able to say, for any claim in this paper, whether an ablation number backs it or a hypothesis does.

The argument on this page is that if annotated data is the binding constraint, then the right thing to buy with unlabelled text is a starting point for the weights — not an extra term in the loss, and not a separate bank of frozen features. Everything else follows from that commitment: the family it claims, the neighbours it argues against, and why the second stage is so short.

### Designing backwards from the constraint

The opening premise is [[labeled-data-scarcity]]: raw text is abundant, while the annotated set for any single task is small and expensive to build. [[two-stage-training-procedure]] only earns its extra machinery under that asymmetry. If every task came with enough labels, a pre-training stage would have nothing to sell.

The paper then places itself rather than claiming new ground. It calls its work an instance of [[semi-supervised-learning-for-nlp]], a family the related-work section splits in two. In [[unsupervised-pretraining]], unlabelled data chooses where the weights start. In [[auxiliary-training-objectives]], initialization is left alone and an unsupervised term is added to the supervised loss. This recipe sits in the first branch and borrows from the second, since [[auxiliary-lm-objective]] keeps the language modelling loss running during fine-tuning at $\lambda = 0.5$.

Inside the first branch it draws two contrasts. [[word-embedding-transfer]] moves one vector per word into a model that is otherwise trained from scratch; the paper says it wants more than word-level information. [[feature-based-transfer]], and [[elmo-deep-contextualized-word-representations|ELMo]] as its best-known case, freezes a pre-trained model and feeds its hidden states as extra inputs to a task network built separately. The paper's stated objection is [[per-task-parameter-cost]]: that route needs a substantial block of freshly initialized parameters for every new task, whereas here [[minimal-extra-parameters|the only additions]] are the output matrix $W_y$ and embeddings for the delimiter tokens.

### Why stage two is small

The two stages train the same $\Theta$ against different targets. [[generative-pretraining]] maximizes the probability of the next token over unlabelled text. [[supervised-fine-tuning]] maximizes the probability of the correct label given the input. Stage two does not restart; it continues from exactly the parameters stage one produced.

That is why the settings back off instead of starting over. [[pre-training-optimization]] runs Adam at a peak of 2.5e-4, on minibatches of 64 sequences, for 100 passes over BooksCorpus. [[fine-tuning-lr-and-batch]] uses 6.25e-5 on batches of 32 — multiply 6.25e-5 by four and you land on the pre-training peak. [[three-epochs-fine-tuning|Three epochs]] is the whole second stage, against a hundred in the first, and [[classifier-dropout]] at rate 0.1 on the new head is the only regularizer stage two adds.

The paper groups [[ulmfit]], which adapts a pre-trained LSTM through a carefully staged schedule, with the intricate learning schemes it wants to avoid. Its own [[fine-tuning-hyperparameters|schedule]] is one learning rate, a 0.2% warmup, linear decay, done. It files its recipe with the earlier work of the same shape, [[lm-pretraining-then-finetuning-predecessors]].

### How much of this is measured

One link in the chain is measured directly. [[ablation-no-pretraining|Removing pre-training]] and training the same transformer on the supervised tasks costs 14.8% across the board in [[table-5]] — its own number for what the starting point is worth.

The rest is thinner than it reads. The paper reports 6.25e-5 and three epochs and says the model fine-tunes quickly. It sweeps neither setting, so "the small step protects the pre-trained weights" is a reading of the numbers, not a result. The comparison against feature-based transfer is an argument about parameter counts, not a controlled experiment: ELMo appears only inside baselines that differ in architecture and pre-training corpus at once. And [[choice-of-pretraining-objective|which unsupervised objective transfers best]] is named as an open question in the introduction and left open — nothing here tests an alternative to language modelling.

One result cuts against the framing. If pre-training is what rescues small labelled sets, the scarcest set should benefit most, but on [[rte]] — 2490 training examples — the model reaches 56% against 61.7% for a multi-task biLSTM.

The argument stage one makes is that one decision — predict the next token — settles almost everything else about the network. The paper does not present the loss and the architecture as two independent choices; it writes the loss down first, and most of the architecture is what survives once that loss is taken literally.

Begin with the decision itself. The introduction names [[choice-of-pretraining-objective|which unsupervised objective transfers best]] as an open question, listing language modelling, machine translation and discourse coherence as candidates that each beat the others on different tasks. [[language-modeling-objective|Next-token log-likelihood]] is this paper's answer, set out in [[eq-lm-objective|Equation 1]]. As an estimator it is unremarkable: sum the log-probability the network gives each token that actually occurred, and maximize by stochastic gradient descent. That is [[maximum-likelihood-training]] with nothing added on top.

### What the loss forces

$L_1$ conditions each token on the $k$ tokens before it, and the paper trains every position of a sequence in one pass. If a position could attend to the token it is being asked to predict, the loss would be minimized by copying. Hence [[masked-self-attention]]: each position sees itself and earlier positions only. That mask is what turns one forward pass over 512 tokens into 512 predictions that have not seen their own answers.

The mask also removes the encoder. There is no separate source sequence to encode when the input is the model's own past, so the paper keeps a [[decoder-only-stack]] and drops the other half. The [[multi-layer-transformer-decoder]] is therefore a cut of [[transformer-gpt1]], not a redesign of it.

[[eq-decoder-stack|Equation 2]] supplies the remaining three lines. Layer zero is [[input-representation-h0|$h_0 = UW_e + W_p$]]: rows of the [[token-embedding-matrix|token embedding matrix $W_e$]] plus [[learned-position-embeddings|a trained position vector]] per slot, because attention alone sees a set and not an order. Choosing a trained table over fixed sinusoids has a consequence the prose does not spell out: the table has one row per slot, so the [[context-window-512-tokens|512-token window]] is a parameter count, not a runtime setting. The top line multiplies the final states by $W_e^T$ and softmaxes — [[output-softmax-tied-embeddings|the output head is the input table read backwards]] — and since the rows are subword pieces from [[byte-pair-encoding-gpt1|byte-pair encoding]] with 40,000 merges, the predicted distribution is over those pieces.

The sizes then fill in slots the architecture leaves open. States are [[hidden-state-dimension-768|768-dimensional]], and [[twelve-attention-heads|twelve heads]] divide rather than duplicate them: $768/12 = 64$ dimensions each. The [[position-wise-feedforward-3072|feed-forward sublayer]] goes 768 up to 3072 and back, a fourfold widening. Two settings are justified by other settings: [[weight-initialization|$\mathcal{N}(0, 0.02)$]] is called sufficient because [[layer-normalization-gpt1|layernorm]] rescales activations everywhere, and [[decoupled-weight-decay|the modified L2 term]] at $w = 0.01$ is the variant written for [[adam-optimizer-gpt1|Adam]], whose per-parameter step would otherwise rescale a plain penalty unevenly. [[residual-embedding-attention-dropout|Dropout at 0.1]] appears at three points, which is all the paper specifies about [[dropout-gpt1|dropout]] here.

### Where the chain is reasoning, not measurement

The step from $L_1$ to masking is the paper's own logic and is tight. The step from masking to a decoder-only stack is mine as much as theirs — the paper states the choice rather than arguing it.

Everything after that is unmeasured within stage one. No ablation isolates weight tying, learned versus sinusoidal positions, the head count, or the 512-token window. The only number stage one reports on its own terms is [[token-level-perplexity|18.4 perplexity]] on BooksCorpus, which shows the corpus was fit, not that these particular choices caused the fit. The contrast with [[elmo-deep-contextualized-word-representations|ELMo]] is likewise argued, not tested: masking gives up right-hand context in exchange for one stack that can be fine-tuned whole, and the paper never measures what that trade cost.

The paper argues that a pre-trained model can only hand a target task the kind of structure it was able to see during pre-training. Three separate choices — the architecture, the corpus, and the size of the context window — are each justified by the same goal, which is conditioning a prediction on information sitting far back in the text.

The chain starts as a complaint about other people's work. Reviewing the closest prior methods, the paper says their use of LSTM models "restricts their prediction ability to a short range" ([[lstm-short-range-limitation]]). Its own [[multi-layer-transformer-decoder]] is offered as the answer, on the stated grounds that attention gives a more structured memory for long-term dependencies than recurrence does.

Then comes the step that is easy to skip. An architecture that *can* reach far back buys nothing if the training text has no far-back structure in it. So the corpus is picked to supply that: [[bookscorpus]], over 7,000 unpublished books, whose selling point in this paper is [[long-range-contiguous-text|long stretches of contiguous text]]. The paper names the alternative it turned down, [[one-billion-word-benchmark|the 1B Word Benchmark]], as approximately the same size but shuffled at the sentence level. Same token budget, different shape. The choice is an argument about structure, not about scale.

The window is the third piece. In [[eq-lm-objective]], the [[language-modeling-objective|pre-training loss]] conditions each token on the $k$ tokens before it, with $k$ left as a free symbol. The setup section fixes it at [[context-window-512-tokens|512 tokens]], and trains on minibatches of 64 randomly sampled contiguous sequences of that length. On a sentence-shuffled corpus those 512 slots would mostly hold unrelated neighbours; on books they usually hold several paragraphs of one story.

What all three are supposed to capture is named concretely: [[long-range-dependencies-gpt1|relationships spanning many tokens]], such as [[coreference|a pronoun and the name it stands for]] several sentences back, or a question and the passage detail that answers it. The evaluation is then picked to need them. [[race-dataset|RACE]] is chosen over [[cnn-and-squad-contrast|CNN and SQuAD]] because it "has been shown to contain more reasoning type questions", which the paper calls "the perfect evaluation for our model which is trained to handle long-range contexts."

### What the evidence actually reaches

[[token-level-perplexity|A token-level perplexity of 18.4]] shows that [[generative-pretraining|stage one]] fit BooksCorpus. It says nothing about how far back the model looks, and nothing about transfer.

[[table-3]] carries the payoff: 8.9 points on Story Cloze and 5.7 on RACE over the previous best. The paper reads these as demonstrating "the ability of our model to handle long-range contexts effectively." That reading is inferential. Neither benchmark separates items that need distant context from items answerable from a nearby sentence, so the margin is consistent with the claim without isolating it.

The architecture half does get a controlled test. Swapping in a single-layer LSTM costs [[ablation-lstm-substitution|5.6 average score points]] in [[table-5]].

### What was never run

The corpus half has no ablation. No model was pre-trained on the shuffled 1B Word Benchmark and rerun, so the contiguity argument rests on downstream scores from a single training recipe rather than on a comparison.

My reading, not the paper's: the LSTM ablation moves capacity and architecture together — a single-layer 2048-unit LSTM against a 12-layer transformer — and the paper attributes the whole 5.6 to architecture.

[[domain-mismatch-tolerance]] sits underneath all of this. Fiction is used to prepare a model for science-exam entailment, news paraphrase and [[qqp|Quora question pairs]]. The paper states that assumption and the results are consistent with it, but nothing here tests it on its own.

The paper argues that the work of adapting to a task does not have to live in the architecture — it can live in how the input is written down. Every structured input is rewritten as one ordered run of tokens, so the same pre-trained stack reads every task, and the only machinery added on top is a single matrix.

### From four input shapes to one vector

The chain starts with a mismatch. The pre-trained network is a [[multi-layer-transformer-decoder]], and Section 3.3 says it was trained on contiguous sequences of text. The evaluation tasks do not hand over contiguous text: entailment gives an ordered sentence pair, and reading comprehension gives a document, a question and a set of candidate answers.

The paper names the route it is not taking. Prior work put [[task-specific-architectures]] on top of transferred representations, and the objection given is that those added components are freshly initialized, so transfer buys them nothing.

The alternative is the [[traversal-style-approach]]: walk the parts of a structured input into one sequence. That is the whole content of [[task-specific-input-transformations]]. [[entailment-input-transformation|Entailment]] concatenates premise and hypothesis with a `$` between them, and the model is never told there were two sentences. The [[qa-and-commonsense-input-transformation|question-answering case]] does not flatten at all, so the paper builds `[z; q; $; a_k]` once per candidate answer, runs each through the same stack, and softmaxes the resulting scores across candidates. Variable structure is absorbed by running the fixed model several times. [[fig-1]] draws all four shapes feeding one stack.

Now the readout. Whatever the sequence was, the classifier sees exactly one vector: [[final-token-activation]], the final block's output at the last input token. Every transformed input is bracketed by [[start-and-end-tokens]], which makes that last position the same kind of token in every example — the paper states the bracketing as part of the transformations rather than arguing this consequence, so the connection is my reading of it.

That single vector is what makes the head small. [[eq-task-head]] is $\mathrm{softmax}(h_l^m W_y)$, so the entire task-specific classifier is [[linear-output-layer-wy|one matrix]]. [[eq-supervised-objective|Equation 4]] then states [[supervised-objective-l2|the loss]] as the summed log-probability of the correct labels — ordinary supervised training, nothing task-shaped in it. The paper's own summary of [[supervised-fine-tuning]] follows: the [[minimal-extra-parameters|only extra parameters]] are $W_y$ and embeddings for the delimiter tokens.

Two claims land from this. One architecture is a [[task-agnostic-model]] across all twelve datasets, and the [[per-task-parameter-cost]] of a new task is one matrix plus a couple of embeddings.

### What the design is and is not shown to do

The outcome numbers are real: new best results on 9 of 12 datasets against [[baseline-comparisons|mostly task-built biLSTM systems]], including 8.9% absolute on Story Cloze, 5.7% on RACE and 5.8% on QNLI, beating ensembles in several cases. On RTE the model gets 56% against a multi-task biLSTM's 61.7%.

What those numbers do not isolate is the transformation scheme itself. The paper never runs a task-specific architecture on top of its own pre-trained stack, so the comparison in Section 3.3 is against other people's systems, not a controlled swap. The ablations test pre-training, the transformer-versus-LSTM choice and the auxiliary objective — not the serialization.

The [[similarity-input-transformation]] is the clearest case. The last-token readout is order-sensitive, so the paper builds both orderings and adds the two final activations element-wise, at twice the compute per example. The motive is stated plainly; the one-ordering control that would price the repair is not reported.

The parameter-cost comparison is likewise qualitative. [[feature-based-transfer|Feature-based transfer]] is described as needing "a substantial amount of new parameters" per task, with no count set beside $W_y$.

The paper's second training stage carries two losses at once, and its analysis section removes three pieces of the recipe one at a time to find out which pieces the results actually rest on. The removals produce a ranking: pre-training first by a wide margin, the transformer second, and the extra loss third — third because its effect does not have one sign.

### Two losses over the same weights

Fine-tuning starts from a task loss. [[supervised-objective-l2|$L_2$]] sums the log-probability of the correct label over the labelled data.

The paper does not optimize that alone. It keeps computing the pre-training language modelling loss on the labelled task's own inputs and adds it in, as [[eq-combined-objective|$L_3(C) = L_2(C) + \lambda L_1(C)$]]. The [[auxiliary-objective-weight|weight $\lambda$]] is set to 0.5, so the language modelling term is counted at half the strength of the label term. Two objectives now pull on the same weights.

Keeping the second one costs almost nothing in parameters. The language modelling head is not a separate matrix: the model scores next tokens with [[output-softmax-tied-embeddings|$\mathrm{softmax}(h_n W_e^T)$]], the transpose of the [[token-embedding-matrix]] it already carries. So the head survives from stage one without anyone deciding to keep it.

The related work files this move under a branch of semi-supervised learning it names [[auxiliary-training-objectives|auxiliary training objectives]], where the added unsupervised loss *is* the transfer mechanism. Here it is not the mechanism. It rides on top of [[generative-pretraining|pre-training]], and the paper's reason is that pre-training has already learned the linguistic aspects such an objective would otherwise supply. Section 3.2 says the [[auxiliary-lm-objective|auxiliary objective]] helps by improving generalization and by speeding up convergence. Neither of those two effects is measured separately anywhere in the paper.

### Three removals, one ranking

[[table-5]] takes the full recipe and knocks out one piece per row.

Remove [[ablation-no-pretraining|pre-training]] and train the identical transformer directly on the supervised tasks. Performance falls on every task measured, 14.8% below the full model. That row is the strongest single piece of evidence the paper has for the [[two-stage-training-procedure|two-stage design]].

Now swap the [[multi-layer-transformer-decoder|transformer]] for a single-layer 2048-unit LSTM. The average score drops [[ablation-lstm-substitution|5.6 points]]. The swap is a clean comparison because [[task-specific-input-transformations|the input transformations]] are architecture-independent — same serialized sequences, same last-token readout, same objectives — so the sequence model is what changed. [[mrpc|MRPC]] is the one dataset where the LSTM comes out ahead.

Set 14.8 against 5.6. By the paper's own measurement, the pre-training matters about three times as much as the architecture choice.

Then remove the auxiliary loss. The result is not a uniform drop: [[ablation-no-auxiliary-objective|it helps on the NLI tasks and QQP and does not help elsewhere]], which the paper reads as larger datasets benefiting and smaller ones not.

### Where the evidence is thinner than the claim

The size trend is the paper's own reading of a handful of dataset scores in one table. It is not a controlled study that holds a task fixed and varies training-set size.

$\lambda$ is fixed at 0.5 for every task, with no sweep reported. So the one removal whose sign changes with dataset size was run at a single weight across all the cases where the evidence says the balance should differ. Whether a per-task $\lambda$ would close the split is untested here — that reading is mine, not the paper's.

Two more gaps, also my reading rather than the paper's. The LSTM has one layer and 2048 units against twelve layers of 768; no parameter or compute matching is stated, so 5.6 points mixes architecture with capacity. And the fine-tuning settings — three epochs, learning rate 6.25e-5 — were chosen for a pre-trained model, then inherited by the row that has no pre-training to fine-tune.

The paper's result is one number: new best published results on nine of twelve datasets. That number is not measured anywhere in the paper — it is a count assembled by reading three separate tables — and this page follows how it is built, what it leaves out, and where the paper's own explanation of its failures does not hold.

### Building the count

The denominator comes first. [[table-1]] lays out [[evaluation-task-families|four task families across twelve datasets]], so the count has a fixed base before any result is reported.

The numerator is spread across three tables. [[table-2]] covers [[natural-language-inference]] and reports the fine-tuned model ahead on four of five datasets: 1.5% on [[multinli|MNLI]], 5% on SciTail, 5.8% on QNLI and 0.6% on SNLI. [[table-3]] adds two more, with margins of 8.9% on the [[story-cloze-test]] and 5.7% overall on RACE, the paper's largest and the two the abstract leads with. [[table-4]] contributes three: [[cola]], [[sts-b]] and [[qqp]].

Four plus two plus three is nine. The three that are left over are [[rte]], [[sst-2]], and — by subtraction from the claim of state-of-the-art on two of the three [[semantic-similarity]] datasets — [[mrpc]]. The paper names the first two in the text and never names the third.

A count also flattens the margins. The 0.6% on SNLI and the 8.9% on Story Cloze each contribute exactly one to the nine, even though the paper reports its gains as [[absolute-improvement|absolute percentage-point differences]] and those two differ by more than a factor of ten.

### Where the general claim thins

[[rte]] is the clearest gap. The model reaches 56% against 61.7% from a multi-task biLSTM, so it falls 5.7 points short of the previous best on the one NLI dataset it loses.

The paper's explanation is dataset size: RTE has 2490 training examples, and it suggests the model would likely benefit from multi-task training too. It then says plainly that it has not run that experiment. The explanation is a hypothesis, not a result.

The explanation also sits awkwardly beside the section's closing sentence, which says the approach works well across dataset sizes from STS-B at roughly 5.7k examples up to [[snli]] at roughly 550k. RTE at 2490 is smaller than either endpoint of that stated range. Reading those two passages together — the paper does not connect them itself — the size claim is made over the datasets that support it, while the one dataset below the range is the one that fails.

One arithmetic gap is worth checking directly. Section 4.2 reports an overall [[glue-benchmark]] score of 72.8 against a previous best of 68.9, a difference of 3.9 points, while the introduction claims 5.5% on GLUE. The paper does not reconcile the two figures.

### How strong is each link

The dataset-size reading of RTE and the untested multi-task suggestion are the paper's own, and it hedges both. The observation that RTE is smaller than the range the paper claims to cover is my reading of two sentences it keeps apart.

Two interpretations rest on assertion rather than measurement. The paper reads the CoLA jump from 35.0 to 45.4 as showing the linguistic bias the model learned, but a single score does not separate that from any other reason for the gain — and [[sst-2]] at 91.3%, competitive but not ahead, is the other [[text-classification]] task and gets no such reading. Likewise, the NLI margins are said to demonstrate reasoning over multiple sentences and handling of linguistic ambiguity; no experiment in the paper isolates either capability.

The analysis section asks a different question from the rest of the paper: not whether the two-stage recipe wins, but why it does. Its answer comes in two halves — transferable function is spread through the whole depth of the stack rather than sitting in the embedding table, and task-relevant behaviour accumulates during pre-training while only the language modelling loss is being optimized.

### Every layer holds something

[[layers-transferred|The layer-transfer sweep]] fine-tunes on MultiNLI and RACE while varying how many pre-trained layers are carried across, from the embeddings alone up to the full stack. That sweep is a dial with twelve settings only because the model is [[twelve-layer-depth|twelve blocks deep]]. A shallower model would leave fewer points on the curve.

The left panel of [[fig-2]] shows dev accuracy climbing with each additional layer, and the paper puts the gap at up to 9% for full transfer on MultiNLI. The bottom of that curve reproduces a known result: [[word-embedding-transfer|transferring word embeddings]] helps. The rest is the paper's own point — stopping at the embedding table gives up most of the available gain.

### The model scoring itself

The second half needs a device first. A generative model emits a distribution over next tokens, not task labels, so making it answer anything without [[supervised-fine-tuning|fine-tuning]] means turning it into a scorer.

[[average-token-log-probability-scoring|The scoring rule]] is: take a candidate string, ask the model for the log-probability of each of its tokens, and average them. That number is the same quantity [[language-modeling-objective|$L_1$]] maximizes in [[eq-lm-objective]], read out over one candidate instead of summed over a corpus.

Three of the four heuristics are that one rule pointed at different spans of text. [[cola-zero-shot-heuristic|CoLA]] thresholds a sentence's mean score to predict grammaticality. [[race-zero-shot-heuristic|RACE]] conditions on the document and question, then keeps the highest-scoring candidate answer. [[dprd-winograd-heuristic|DPRD]] substitutes each possible referent for the definite pronoun and keeps the resolution whose remaining text scores higher, turning a [[coreference]] question into a comparison between two rewritten sentences.

[[sst2-zero-shot-heuristic|SST-2]] works another way, appending the token 'very' and restricting [[output-softmax-tied-embeddings|the output distribution]] to 'positive' and 'negative'. No classifier is trained anywhere in any of this.

Because the read-out is the training quantity, [[zero-shot-behaviors|these heuristics]] can be tracked across pre-training updates. The right panel of the figure shows their scores rising steadily and staying stable, which the paper takes as [[generative-pretraining|pre-training]] supporting a wide variety of task-relevant functionality.

### What the diagnostic does not settle

The curves are relative trends over training, not absolute task scores. They are evidence that the ability grows; they are not evidence that it is competitive with the fine-tuned numbers, and the paper does not claim otherwise. Its own wording is "suggesting", not "showing".

Two claims run further than the plot. [[transformer-inductive-bias|The structured-memory hypothesis]] rests on one observation: [[lstm-gpt1|the LSTM]] shows higher variance in the same zero-shot measurements. No variance figure is quoted, so this is a qualitative reading of a curve rather than a measurement, and the paper states it as a hypothesis.

The conclusion's [[world-knowledge|claim about world knowledge]] is broader still. The nearest supporting evidence is the zero-shot panel plus the downstream scores, and neither measures facts about the world directly.

My own reading of the layer sweep is similarly limited: it shows depth helps on two datasets, and says nothing about what any individual layer contains.

Deep models for the tasks the paper groups under [[natural-language-understanding]] are normally fitted on examples that a person labelled by hand. The paper's opening claim is that there are not nearly enough of those examples, and this page comes first because every later design choice is an answer to that shortage.

Put the two resources side by side with real numbers. The evaluation includes [[rte]], an inference dataset with 2,490 training examples, and [[sts-b]], a similarity dataset with roughly 5,700. The largest labelled set anywhere in the evaluation, [[snli]], has about 550,000.

Against those figures, the pre-training corpus [[bookscorpus]] is over 7,000 unpublished books of running prose. Nobody annotated a word of it. The text was written for its own reasons and was already there.

So the asymmetry is not only in size. It is in cost per example: an annotated pair has to be commissioned from a person, while a sentence of raw text is free.

### What the shortage costs

A model trained only to predict a label given an input — the discriminative framing set out in [[generative-vs-discriminative-training]] — has to learn everything from those pairs. With RTE that means estimating how English sentences relate to each other from 2,490 examples. Capacity the labelled data cannot fill goes into memorising it instead.

This is the asymmetry [[two-stage-training-procedure]] is designed backwards from. Spend the plentiful resource to relieve the scarce one: let unlabelled text decide where the weights start, so the labelled set only has to adjust a model that already reads, rather than build one from nothing. If every task had 550,000 examples, the extra stage would buy little.

The paper adds a second, softer motive. Even where supervision is plentiful, it says, learning representations without labels still gives a boost — and the evidence offered for that is the existing record of [[word-embedding-transfer]] inside [[semi-supervised-learning-for-nlp]], not anything measured here.

### How strong the evidence is

The direct test is [[ablation-no-pretraining]] in [[table-5]]: the same transformer, the same fine-tuning, with stage one removed costs 14.8% on average. That isolates pre-training cleanly.

It does not isolate scarcity, though. There is no curve of performance against labelled-set size, so the 14.8% is an average over twelve datasets rather than a demonstration that small datasets are where the gain lives.

[[table-2]] complicates it further. RTE, the smallest set in the evaluation, is the one inference dataset where the model loses — 56% against 61.7% for a multi-task biLSTM. On the simplest reading of the scarcity story, that is exactly where the gain should have been largest.

Semi-supervised learning for NLP means training on a large unlabelled corpus and a small labelled dataset for the same end task. The paper opens its related-work section by claiming this category outright, because [[labeled-data-scarcity|annotation is the binding constraint]] and it needs to say which of several existing answers to that constraint it is adopting.

The category fixes what may move. The task, its labels and its metric stay exactly as they were. Unlabelled text is allowed to change the model — its input features, its loss, or its starting weights — but not the definition of the problem.

### The sorting axis

The paper's split is about *where* the unlabelled text enters, and it walks the branches roughly in order of when they appeared.

The oldest branch computes word- and phrase-level counts from raw text and appends them as features to a supervised model. [[word-embedding-transfer]] replaced those counts with learned vectors, and [[phrase-and-sentence-embeddings]] pushed the same idea up to longer spans. The delivery mechanism does not change across that progression: something is computed once on unlabelled text, then handed to a task model that is otherwise trained from the labelled set alone.

The paper's objection is specific. A table of one vector per word moves word-level information and nothing else; whatever composes those words into meaning is still learned from the small dataset.

Two other branches exist. [[auxiliary-training-objectives]] add an unsupervised loss term next to the supervised one. [[unsupervised-pretraining]] leaves the objective alone and uses unlabelled data only to pick the initialization — this is where the paper puts itself, and [[two-stage-training-procedure|its own recipe is one member of that branch]], not a new category.

Inside that branch it draws one more line. [[feature-based-transfer]] freezes the pre-trained model and feeds its states into a separate task network, which means [[per-task-parameter-cost|fresh parameters for every task]]. [[lm-pretraining-then-finetuning-predecessors]] instead fine-tunes the whole network, and the paper calls this the closest work to its own; its disagreement there is architectural, not procedural, and rests on the [[lstm-short-range-limitation|claim that recurrence keeps predictions local]].

### How much of this is shown

Almost none of it, in this section. Related work argues; the numbers arrive later.

Two claims do get a measurement. [[table-5]] reports that removing pre-training costs 14.8 average points, and that substituting a single-layer 2048-unit LSTM costs 5.6. The second is one substitution at one size inside this paper's own pipeline, not a study of what recurrence can carry.

The claim about capturing more than word-level semantics is never tested against word embeddings directly. [[fig-2]]'s layer-transfer curve is the nearest thing to support.

Train one network to predict the next token on unlabelled text, then keep training that same network on a labelled task. The procedure exists because of the asymmetry the paper opens with: raw text is abundant, while [[labeled-data-scarcity|annotated data for any one task]] is small and expensive, so the unlabelled corpus is asked to pay for what annotation cannot.

The paper does not claim a new category for this. It places the recipe inside [[semi-supervised-learning-for-nlp]], as one particular member of that family — the one where unlabelled data chooses where the weights start rather than adding a term to the supervised loss.

### What actually crosses the boundary

Stage one, [[generative-pretraining]], maximizes the [[language-modeling-objective|likelihood $L_1$]] over a corpus of tokens. The output it cares about is not a prediction. It is $\Theta$: every weight of the twelve-block, 768-dimensional decoder described in [[model-specification]].

Stage two, [[supervised-fine-tuning]], loads those same weights and continues from them. A labelled input runs through the stack, the final block's activation at the last token is read off, and one added matrix [[linear-output-layer-wy|$W_y$]] maps it to label scores under [[supervised-objective-l2|$L_2$]].

Count what stage two adds. For a three-way label, $W_y$ is $768 \times 3$, so 2304 fresh weights — against a whole pre-trained stack whose every weight is also updated by the same backward pass. Nothing is frozen, and no task-specific network is built on top.

That is the line the paper draws against [[feature-based-transfer]], where the pre-trained model stays fixed and its hidden states are fed to a separate task model as inputs. Here the parameters themselves move, which is what makes it [[transfer-learning]] rather than feature extraction. Keeping the architecture fixed across twelve datasets is only possible because [[structured-inputs]] are flattened first — see [[task-specific-input-transformations]]. The paper also assumes the corpus need not match the target domain ([[domain-mismatch-tolerance]]).

### How strong the evidence is

The load-bearing number is in [[table-5]]: the same transformer trained directly on the supervised tasks, with no stage one, drops 14.8% across the board. That is one controlled removal, reported as an average with no variance across seeds, but it is a genuine ablation and it isolates the recipe.

The same table complicates it. Swapping the transformer for an LSTM costs 5.6, so part of the margin belongs to the backbone rather than to the two stages. [[fig-2]] adds that each transferred layer helps, up to 9% on MultiNLI.

The scoreboards — [[table-2]], [[table-4]] — measure the whole package against differently built systems, and lose on RTE, SST-2 and [[mrpc]]. They show the recipe is competitive; they do not, on their own, show which part of it works.

Stage one trains a single network against a single loss: predict the next token, over a corpus that carries no labels anywhere in it. It is here because [[supervised-fine-tuning|stage two]] needs somewhere to start, and next-token prediction is the one objective that scales to the amount of text that exists.

The training signal is written out in [[eq-lm-objective]]. The [[language-modeling-objective|objective $L_1$]] walks every position $i$ in the corpus, reads off the log-probability the network assigns to the actual token $u_i$ given the $k$ tokens immediately before it, and sums those numbers. Gradient ascent on that sum is the whole of stage one. Here $k$ is [[context-window-512-tokens|512 contiguous tokens]], so a prediction can condition on material several paragraphs back.

The conditional itself is computed by a [[multi-layer-transformer-decoder]], and the [[model-specification|trained configuration]] is twelve blocks, 768-dimensional states, twelve heads, and 3072-dimensional inner feed-forward states.

It is worth walking what one update contains. A minibatch is 64 sampled sequences of 512 tokens, so 32,768 token positions go through the stack at once. Each of those positions contributes its own term to $L_1$. No part of that batch had to be annotated by anyone.

### Why pay for this

The [[pre-training-optimization|optimization run]] makes 100 passes over [[bookscorpus|BooksCorpus]], which the paper picks for [[long-range-contiguous-text|unbroken stretches of text]] rather than for size. Nothing about the target tasks enters. When it finishes, the output distribution is thrown away and only $\Theta$ moves forward, which is what makes this an instance of [[unsupervised-pretraining|weight-initializing]] rather than loss-shaping semi-supervision. It also separates the method from [[word-embedding-transfer]], which moves one vector per word instead of every layer.

The cost is paid entirely up front. Those 100 epochs buy a stage two of [[three-epochs-fine-tuning|three epochs]] at [[fine-tuning-lr-and-batch|a learning rate four times smaller]] — a budget that only makes sense as an adjustment to weights already worth keeping.

### How strong the evidence is

The direct number is the [[ablation-no-pretraining|no-pre-training ablation]] in [[table-5]]: the same transformer trained straight on the supervised tasks loses 14.8 points on average. That isolates stage one cleanly and is the paper's strongest single result for it.

The rest is weaker. [[fig-2]] shows zero-shot task scores climbing during pre-training, which the paper offers as a reason the recipe works, and words as a hypothesis. The reported [[token-level-perplexity|perplexity of 18.4]] says the model fit BooksCorpus, not that the fit transfers. The conclusion's claim about acquired [[world-knowledge]] is asserted rather than measured.

$L_1$ is the loss that trains stage one, and it is the only loss stage one has. It is here because the paper wants a training signal that costs no annotation, so that a large corpus of raw text can set the network's starting weights before any labelled task appears.

### The operation

Fix a position $i$ in the corpus. The model reads the $k$ tokens immediately before it, $u_{i-k},\dots,u_{i-1}$, and emits one distribution over the whole vocabulary. That vocabulary is the byte-pair set built with 40,000 merges, so the softmax spreads mass over roughly forty thousand entries.

The objective then reads a single number off that distribution: the log-probability it placed on $u_i$, the token that actually came next. [[eq-lm-objective]] sums that number over every position in the corpus and maximizes the sum by stochastic gradient descent on the parameters $\Theta$. Nothing about the estimator goes past [[maximum-likelihood-training]] — what is new in stage one is the corpus and the network, not the fitting. The three lines that turn a context into the distribution are [[eq-decoder-stack]].

Now the shapes. $k$ is fixed at 512 ([[context-window-512-tokens]]), and each minibatch holds 64 such sequences, so a single gradient step carries $64 \times 512 = 32{,}768$ separate prediction terms.

That density depends on [[masked-self-attention]]. Without the mask, a position could attend to the token it is being asked to predict, and the objective would be satisfied by copying. Every forward pass would then yield one honest prediction rather than 512.

### What the choice costs

The introduction is explicit that nobody knows which unsupervised objective produces representations that transfer best, and it names language modelling, machine translation and discourse coherence as candidates that each lead on different tasks ([[choice-of-pretraining-objective]]). Next-token likelihood is this paper's pick, not its argument. It reports what happens when you use it.

The price is the strict left-to-right conditioning. A token's representation never sees anything to its right, at any layer, at any point in pre-training.

### How strong the evidence is

On [[bookscorpus]] the trained model reaches a token-level perplexity of 18.4 ([[token-level-perplexity]]). Perplexity is $L_1$ restated on a per-token scale, so that figure says the corpus was fitted well.

It is one number on the pre-training corpus, and on its own it says nothing about whether the weights transfer. The claim that they do rests on the fine-tuning results, and most directly on [[ablation-no-pretraining]].

$L_1$ is also not retired when stage one ends; it returns weighted during fine-tuning as the [[auxiliary-lm-objective]].

This is the network that computes the next-token probability in [[language-modeling-objective|the stage-one objective]] — the only thing trained on BooksCorpus, and the thing whose weights are later handed to every task. It is not a new design: it is the [[transformer-gpt1|transformer]] block of prior work, stacked twelve deep and cut down to one side.

### What the three lines compute

[[eq-decoder-stack|Equation 2]] writes the whole network in three lines, and reading it is how you confirm there is no encoder and no cross-attention anywhere in the model.

Line one builds the input. Take the context $U$, up to 512 token ids, look each one up in the [[token-embedding-matrix|token embedding matrix]] $W_e$, and add the [[learned-position-embeddings|position embedding]] for its slot. That gives [[input-representation-h0|$h_0$]], a $512 \times 768$ array of activations.

Line two runs the stack: $h_l = \mathrm{transformer\_block}(h_{l-1})$ for $l \in [1, n]$, with $n = 12$ in the [[model-specification|trained model]]. Each block does masked multi-head self-attention, then a position-wise feed-forward layer. The 768 dimensions are split across twelve heads, so each head attends in a 64-dimensional subspace; the feed-forward layer widens 768 to 3072 and projects back, a fourfold expansion. The shape entering a block and the shape leaving it are the same, which is what lets you stack identical blocks.

Line three reads the stack out. Multiply $h_n$ by $W_e^{T}$ and softmax, giving a distribution over the vocabulary at each position. The [[output-softmax-tied-embeddings|same matrix does the work at both ends]], so no separate output vocabulary matrix exists.

Two restrictions make this a decoder rather than a transformer: the encoder half is [[decoder-only-stack|dropped entirely]], and attention is [[masked-self-attention|masked]] so position $i$ sees only positions $\le i$.

### Why a transformer, and how firmly that is shown

The paper's stated reason is that recurrent pre-trained models keep their predictions [[lstm-short-range-limitation|short-range]], which caps how much structure they can hand to a target task. Attention is offered as the fix. The wider argument depends on it: one stack serving twelve datasets is what makes the model [[task-agnostic-model|task-agnostic]] at all, and [[fig-1]] draws exactly that.

The measurement is one row of [[table-5]]. Holding the rest of the recipe fixed and substituting a single-layer 2048-unit LSTM costs 5.6 average points, and the LSTM wins on one dataset, [[mrpc|MRPC]]. That is a single ablation, at one recurrent configuration, with no parameter matching and no repeated runs reported. The right panel of [[fig-2]] adds a softer signal: zero-shot scores grow more smoothly for the transformer than for an LSTM trained the same way. Note the scale — removing pre-training altogether costs 14.8, so the architecture is the smaller of the two effects the paper measures.

The [[transformer-gpt1|original transformer]] is two stacks. An encoder reads a source sequence with unrestricted self-attention, and a decoder generates a target while attending to its own past through masking and, through a separate cross-attention sublayer, to the encoder's output states.

The [[language-modeling-objective|language modelling objective]] used here has no source sequence. There is nothing to encode, so the paper keeps the decoder side alone and deletes the sublayer that would have had nothing to attend to.

### What is left in one block

Each block is now two sublayers: [[masked-self-attention]] over the context, then a [[position-wise-feedforward-3072|position-wise feed-forward network]].

Follow the shapes. A context of [[context-window-512-tokens|512 tokens]] enters as a $512 \times 768$ matrix — [[input-representation-h0|one row per position]], each row a [[token-embedding-matrix|token embedding]] added to a [[learned-position-embeddings|learned position vector]].

Attention splits those [[hidden-state-dimension-768|768 dimensions]] into [[twelve-attention-heads|12 heads]] of $768/12 = 64$ dimensions each. The feed-forward sublayer then takes each of the 512 rows on its own, widens it from 768 to 3072, and projects it back to 768.

So a block returns exactly the shape it was given. That is why the same block can be stacked [[twelve-layer-depth|twelve times]] with nothing between the copies, and why the top states can be sent straight back through [[output-softmax-tied-embeddings|the transposed embedding matrix]] to score the next token. [[eq-decoder-stack]] writes the whole network in three lines:

$$h_0 = UW_e + W_p, \qquad h_l = \mathrm{transformer\ block}(h_{l-1}), \qquad P(u) = \mathrm{softmax}(h_n W_e^{\top})$$

### What the choice costs

Dropping cross-attention removes the model's only second input port. From here on, anything the model reads — a premise and a hypothesis, a document with a question and a candidate answer — has to arrive as one ordered sequence, which is the work [[task-specific-input-transformations|the input transformations]] are there to do.

The masking is permanent too. No position ever sees its right context, in pre-training or in fine-tuning.
