### How firm the evidence is

The left panel of [[fig-1]] draws the repeated block, and [[model-specification|Section 4.1]] states the configuration flatly: a 12-layer decoder-only transformer with masked self-attention heads. Both are descriptions of what was built, not tests of it.

The one architectural comparison the paper does run is [[table-5]], which replaces the transformer with [[ablation-lstm-substitution|a single-layer 2048-unit LSTM]] and loses 5.6 average points. That weighs attention against recurrence. It says nothing about whether an encoder half would have added anything, and the paper does not argue that it would.

Masked self-attention is the edit that turns a general transformer block into a language model block: before the attention softmax, every score pointing from a position to a position on its right is set to $-\infty$. It is here because [[language-modeling-objective|the pre-training loss $L_1$]] asks the model to predict each token from the tokens before it, and an unmasked block would let a position read the very token it is being scored on.

### The operation

Take one head at one layer. The 512 positions of a [[context-window-512-tokens|training sequence]] produce queries and keys, and their dot products form a $512 \times 512$ score matrix — row $i$ holds position $i$'s affinity for every position in the window.

The mask is an additive term over that matrix. Entries above the diagonal get $-\infty$; the diagonal and everything below it are left alone. Softmax over a row then sends those entries to exactly zero.

So row 400 has 401 non-zero weights and 111 zeros. Position 400 mixes values from tokens 0 through 400 and nothing else — precisely the conditioning set $u_{i-k},\dots,u_i$ that $L_1$ writes down.

This happens independently in each of the [[twelve-attention-heads|twelve heads]], each working in a 64-dimensional slice of the [[hidden-state-dimension-768|768-dimensional state]], at all [[twelve-layer-depth|twelve layers]]. That is 144 masked score matrices per forward pass, all sharing one triangular pattern.

The payoff is throughput. One pass over 512 tokens yields 512 predictions that are all honest, rather than one prediction per pass, because no position could have peeked.

### What it costs

The mask is what makes [[decoder-only-stack|a single stack with no encoder]] coherent, but it buys that by giving up the right context permanently. A token's representation never sees what follows it. [[elmo-deep-contextualized-word-representations|ELMo]] makes the opposite trade: its pre-trained language model reads both directions, and pays by not being a single stack you can fine-tune as-is.

The mask also does not lift at fine-tuning time. Only the last position has seen the whole input, which is why the classifier reads [[final-token-activation|the final block's activation at the last token]] instead of pooling, and why a structured input has to be flattened into [[task-specific-input-transformations|one ordered sequence]] first.

### How well is this shown

Thinly, as a direct claim. The paper states the heads are masked and [[fig-1|the architecture figure]] labels the sublayer, but there is no ablation isolating the mask — nothing in the paper compares masked against unmasked pre-training. The [[token-level-perplexity|perplexity of 18.4]] shows the arrangement trained well; it does not separate the mask's contribution from anything else. The ELMo contrast is a comparison between published systems, not a controlled test.

Stage two continues training the exact weights that [[generative-pretraining|stage one]] left behind, now on a task's labelled examples. It is here because a language model emits distributions over tokens, not labels, and something has to turn its hidden states into a decision about entailment, sentiment, or which candidate answer is right.

### The task head

A target task supplies [[labeled-dataset-c|labelled data $C$]]: each instance is a token sequence $x_1,\dots,x_m$ paired with one label $y$. That sequence is pushed through the same twelve pre-trained blocks used during pre-training, unchanged.

Then take one vector out of the stack: the last block's output at the final position, $h_l^m$, described under [[final-token-activation]]. Multiply it by an added matrix [[linear-output-layer-wy|$W_y$]] and softmax the scores. That is the entire task-specific network, and [[eq-task-head]] is the whole of it on one line.

Walk the sizes. The activation is 768-dimensional ([[hidden-state-dimension-768]]), so for a three-way inference task $W_y$ holds $768 \times 3 = 2304$ numbers, sitting on top of roughly 117 million pre-trained parameters. Adding a task costs about two parameters in a hundred thousand — the point [[minimal-extra-parameters]] makes and [[fig-1]] draws.

The gradient, though, does not stop at $W_y$. Maximizing [[supervised-objective-l2|$L_2$]] ([[eq-supervised-objective]]) backpropagates through all twelve blocks and into the embeddings, so every pre-trained weight moves. That is the difference from [[elmo-deep-contextualized-word-representations|feature-based transfer]], where pre-trained states are frozen features handed to a task network trained from scratch. The target also flips — [[generative-vs-discriminative-training|predict the label, not the text]] — though the paper does not flip it all the way, since [[auxiliary-lm-objective|the language modelling loss keeps running]] alongside.

### What it costs, and how firm the evidence is

Updating a whole 117M-parameter model on a few thousand labelled examples invites overfitting, so the budget is deliberately short: [[fine-tuning-hyperparameters]] give a learning rate of 6.25e-5, batches of 32, and three passes over the data. The paper hedges on that last number — three epochs was "sufficient for most cases", which leaves unnamed tasks needing more. There is also an unstated cost: since all weights change, each task ends up with its own full copy of the model.

The strongest number for why any of this works is the ablation in [[table-5]]. Training the same transformer straight on the supervised tasks, skipping pre-training, drops the average by 14.8% ([[ablation-no-pretraining]]).

That is one run per configuration, on the paper's own dataset selection, with no variance reported. The layer-transfer curve in [[fig-2]] is thinner still: dev accuracy on two datasets, rising to about 9% on MultiNLI at full transfer. It supports "more transferred layers help" rather than any claim about a particular layer.

The next-token loss does not switch off when stage two begins. Fine-tuning maximizes a sum of two losses at once, written out in [[eq-combined-objective|Equation 5]]:

$$L_3(C) = L_2(C) + \lambda\, L_1(C)$$

### What actually gets computed

Take one labelled example from [[labeled-dataset-c|$C$]]: a token sequence $x_1,\dots,x_m$ and its label $y$. A single forward pass through the stack produces a hidden state at each of the $m$ positions.

The state at the last position is multiplied by the added matrix $W_y$ and softmaxed over labels. The log-probability of the correct $y$ is the classification term [[supervised-objective-l2|$L_2$]], given in [[eq-supervised-objective|Equation 4]].

Now read the same sequence as ordinary text and ignore the label. At each position the hidden state is projected to vocabulary scores, and the log-probability of the token that actually came next is read off. Summed over positions, that is [[language-modeling-objective|$L_1$]] — the pre-training loss, recomputed on the task's own inputs instead of on [[bookscorpus|BooksCorpus]].

Both terms come off the same activations, so there is no second forward pass. There are no extra parameters either: the language modelling head is just [[output-softmax-tied-embeddings|the transpose of the token embedding matrix]], which the model is carrying regardless. A method with a separately learned output projection would have to keep that projection alive deliberately for this to be free.

The extra work is that the vocabulary-sized projection now runs at every position rather than only at the last one.

$\lambda$ sets the balance between the two terms. The paper uses 0.5, discussed below in [[auxiliary-objective-weight]].

### Why it is here, and what it costs

Section 3.2 reports two effects from including the term: better generalization of the supervised model, and faster convergence. Both are stated as findings. No mechanism is offered, and the paper points to prior work that saw similar gains from adding a language modelling term to a supervised loss.

The framing is worth pinning down. In [[auxiliary-training-objectives|the auxiliary-objective line of work]], the added unsupervised loss *is* the transfer mechanism. Here it is a secondary term sitting on top of pre-training, and the paper says pre-training has already learned much of what such an objective would otherwise supply.

The cost is a split gradient. Across three passes over the task data, part of the update is pulling towards predicting next tokens rather than labels.

### How strong the evidence is

[[table-5]] reruns the recipe [[ablation-no-auxiliary-objective|without the term]]. Removing it *gains* 0.3 points on average. Keeping it helps on the [[natural-language-inference]] datasets and on [[qqp]], and hurts on the smaller sets; the paper reads that as larger datasets benefiting.

This is thinner than the claim in Section 3.2. It is one run per dataset with no variance reported, and the size rule is inferred after the fact from twelve numbers. The faster-convergence claim is never measured anywhere in the paper.

Pre-training saw one thing: contiguous runs of text, read left to right. Many target tasks do not arrive in that shape, so before [[supervised-fine-tuning|stage two]] can run them through the stack, their parts have to be written out as a single ordered token stream.

[[text-classification]] needs no work. A sentence already is one sequence. [[structured-inputs|The other three families]] — an ordered sentence pair for entailment, an unordered pair for similarity, a document plus question plus candidate answers for multiple choice — need a flattening rule.

### The rule

Concatenate the parts, and mark the seams. Every transformed input is wrapped in [[start-and-end-tokens|a randomly initialized start and end token]], and a [[delimiter-token|`$` delimiter]] sits between adjacent parts. The paper calls this a [[traversal-style-approach|traversal-style approach]], citing earlier work that walks structured input into a sequence.

So [[entailment-input-transformation|entailment]] becomes $\langle s\rangle\,p\;\$\;h\,\langle e\rangle$ — premise tokens, delimiter, hypothesis tokens. Length is the sum of the two pieces plus three. The last position is always $\langle e\rangle$, which is why [[eq-task-head|the linear head]] can always read the same slot.

Two transformations do more than concatenate. [[similarity-input-transformation|Similarity]] builds both orderings and runs each through the model, then adds the two 768-dimensional final activations element-wise before the output layer. [[qa-and-commonsense-input-transformation|Question answering]] builds one sequence per candidate answer and softmaxes across their scores, so a four-option RACE question is four forward passes.

### What it buys and what it costs

The paper's objection to [[task-specific-architectures|task-specific architectures]] is not that they are ugly. It is that a module built on top of transferred representations is freshly initialized, so it gets no benefit from pre-training at all. Rewriting the input instead keeps every parameter that touches the task a pre-trained one, apart from $W_y$ and the delimiter embeddings — which is the whole basis for the [[minimal-extra-parameters|small extra-parameter count]], and for the claim of a [[task-agnostic-model|single model across tasks]].

The costs are real if unmentioned. Compute per example scales with the number of candidates rather than staying at one pass. Document, question and answer must all fit inside [[context-window-512-tokens|the 512-token window]] together. And the new marker embeddings are learned from the labelled set alone, which on RTE means 2,490 examples.

### How strong the evidence is

[[fig-1]]'s right panel draws all four shapes side by side, but it is a specification, not a result. No experiment here isolates serialization against a task-shaped module trained the same way; the support is end-to-end, that the fine-tuned model beats task-built baselines on nine of twelve datasets. That shows the format is sufficient, not that it wins a controlled comparison. What the shared format does buy directly is clean ablation: [[ablation-lstm-substitution|swapping in an LSTM]] varies only the sequence model, since inputs and readout stay fixed ([[table-5]]).

"Task-agnostic" is the claim the paper is making about its own system, not a component of it: one network, pre-trained once, fine-tuned on each of twelve datasets without any of them getting a network of its own. It sits here because everything else in the paper — the pre-training corpus, the objective, the input rewriting — is machinery in service of this one claim.

Concretely, the model is a stack of twelve transformer blocks, the [[multi-layer-transformer-decoder|multi-layer transformer decoder]], with 768-dimensional states. That stack is identical for entailment, for question answering, for similarity and for sentence classification. What each task adds on top is a single matrix, the [[linear-output-layer-wy|added linear output layer $W_y$]], applied to the final block's activation at the last token.

Walk the size of that. A three-way entailment task needs $W_y$ of shape $768 \times 3$, which is 2,304 weights. Alongside it come embeddings for the delimiter tokens. The paper states these are the only extra parameters fine-tuning requires — [[minimal-extra-parameters|minimal extra fine-tuning parameters]].

### Where the task-specific work went

It did not disappear. A model with no structural notion of "sentence pair" can only read a sentence pair if something else makes it look like ordinary text, and that is the job of [[task-specific-input-transformations|task-specific input transformations]]. Premise and hypothesis are concatenated with a delimiter between them; a document, question and candidate answer are walked into one sequence.

So the architecture is task-agnostic because the serialization is task-aware. The paper's contrast is with [[task-specific-architectures|task-specific architectures]], the prevailing practice of hand-designing a network around each task's structure. [[fig-1]] is the visual form of that argument: one block diagram on the left, four differently shaped inputs feeding it on the right.

### How strong the evidence is

The headline is a count: new best published results on [[state-of-the-art-9-of-12|9 of the 12 datasets]] across [[evaluation-task-families|four task families]], including 8.9 points on the [[story-cloze-test]] and 5.7 on RACE. That count is a comparison against a different prior system on each dataset, not a controlled experiment, and each of those systems differs from this one in architecture, in pre-training data and in scale at once. It is breadth, not isolation.

Two of the misses are worth naming: [[rte]], the smallest NLI set at 2,490 examples, and [[mrpc]], where [[ablation-lstm-substitution|swapping in an LSTM]] actually helps. And [[ablation-no-pretraining|removing pre-training]] costs 14.8 average points from the same architecture, which suggests the gains come mostly from what pre-training put in the weights rather than from the architecture being shared.

BooksCorpus is the unlabelled text that stage one actually trains on: over 7,000 unpublished books spanning genres such as Adventure, Fantasy and Romance. It is here because [[generative-pretraining]] needs some corpus of tokens to run [[eq-lm-objective|its likelihood]] over, and the paper picks this one for the shape of its text rather than for its subject matter.

Concretely, the raw text is cleaned and cut into subword units by the [[text-preprocessing-pipeline]], then sliced into training sequences. A minibatch is 64 randomly sampled contiguous runs of 512 tokens each, matching the [[context-window-512-tokens|512-token context window]]. Every one of those 512 positions contributes its own next-token term to the loss, so a single update carries $64 \times 512 = 32{,}768$ predictions. Training makes 100 passes over the corpus at that rate; the schedule is spelled out in [[pretraining-schedule]].

### Why the slicing matters

The word doing the work is *contiguous*. Because a book arrives as one unbroken run of sentences in their original order, a sampled window of 512 tokens is 512 tokens of the same passage. Roughly 400 words of prose, which is several paragraphs.

So a token near the end of that window has up to 511 real predecessors to condition on. Some of the information that would help predict it - who the pronoun refers to, what the scene is - sits paragraphs back. That is what [[long-range-contiguous-text]] buys, and it is how the abstract goal of modelling [[long-range-dependencies-gpt1]] becomes a data-selection decision.

The contrast the paper draws makes the point sharper. The [[one-billion-word-benchmark]] is about the same size, but shuffled sentence by sentence. Fill a 512-token window from it and the history behind any token is a run of unrelated sentences, so conditioning on anything past the current sentence boundary is noise. Same token count, and by the paper's argument a weaker training signal.

### What it costs and what is shown

The corpus is fiction. The evaluation is science exam entailment, news paraphrase and [[qqp|Quora question pairs]]. Bridging that gap rests entirely on [[domain-mismatch-tolerance]], which the paper states as an assumption and does not test with a matched-domain control.

The evidence is thin in a second way too. The paper argues for contiguity but never runs the experiment: there is no ablation pre-training the same model on the shuffled corpus and comparing transfer. The only number offered is [[token-level-perplexity]], and it is measured on BooksCorpus itself. It says the model fit the text it was trained on. The paper does not connect it to any downstream result, and neither should a reader.

This is the configuration the paper actually trained, and every number it reports comes out of this one model. It fills in the free parameters that the [[multi-layer-transformer-decoder|multi-layer transformer decoder]] description leaves open: that description says what kind of network to build, not how big to build it.

The stack is twelve blocks deep ([[twelve-layer-depth]]). Each position carries a 768-dimensional vector from the embedding layer to the top of the stack ([[hidden-state-dimension-768]]). Attention inside a block splits that vector across twelve heads ([[twelve-attention-heads]]), so each head forms queries, keys and values in $768/12 = 64$ dimensions, and the twelve 64-dimensional outputs concatenate back to 768. The feed-forward sublayer widens 768 to 3072 and projects straight back down ([[position-wise-feedforward-3072]]), a factor of four out and back.

Walk the weight count. Attention per block is four $768 \times 768$ projections, about 2.4M parameters. The feed-forward sublayer is two $768 \times 3072$ matrices, about 4.7M. That is roughly 7.1M per block, so about 85M across twelve. The [[byte-pair-encoding-gpt1|BPE]] vocabulary of roughly 40k entries adds another 31M in the embedding table, and 512 learned position slots add 0.4M. Around 117M weights in total — a number the paper itself never states.

### Where it departs from the original transformer

The encoder half is gone ([[decoder-only-stack]]), and attention is masked so a position sees only itself and its past ([[masked-self-attention]]). Position information comes from a trained table rather than fixed sinusoids ([[learned-position-embeddings]]). That table has exactly 512 rows, matching the [[context-window-512-tokens|512-token window]] and going no further. The activation is [[gelu]] rather than ReLU.

[[layer-normalization-gpt1|Layernorm]] is used throughout the stack, and the paper credits that for letting a plain $\mathcal{N}(0, 0.02)$ draw serve as [[weight-initialization|initialization]] with nothing more careful layered on. That is asserted, not tested.

### What supports the numbers

Little, taken as sizes. The paper says it "largely follows" the original transformer and then lists its numbers; there is no sweep over width, depth or head count. The one direct sign the spec fits its job is [[token-level-perplexity|token-level perplexity of 18.4]] on BooksCorpus.

Depth is probed after the fact. The transfer curve in [[fig-2]] varies how many of the twelve layers are carried into fine-tuning ([[layers-transferred]]) and finds each one still adds accuracy. That argues twelve was not too many. It does not argue twelve was right.

The architecture family gets one check, in [[table-5]]: substituting a single-layer 2048-unit LSTM costs 5.6 average points ([[ablation-lstm-substitution]]). Parameter counts are not matched there, so it separates two families more than it isolates the transformer.

The paper trains the language model with [[adam-optimizer-gpt1|Adam]], and reports the optimizer settings in the same breath as the architecture. These are the numbers that turn [[eq-lm-objective|the pre-training likelihood $L_1$]] into an actual set of weights, so they are what a reader would need to rebuild the model that every later experiment starts from.

The learning rate moves in two phases. It starts at zero and rises in a straight line to 2.5e-4 over the first 2000 parameter updates — this is [[linear-warmup|the warmup]]. From there it falls along a cosine curve, reaching zero at the moment training stops, which is [[cosine-annealing|the annealing half]].

That second phase hides a dependency worth naming. A cosine that has to land on zero needs to know in advance where the end of training is. So the length of the run is not a separate knob: [[pretraining-schedule|100 epochs over the corpus]] fixes the horizon the curve is drawn against.

### What one update actually sees

Each minibatch holds 64 sequences. Each sequence is a contiguous span of 512 tokens sampled at random from [[bookscorpus|BooksCorpus]] — a filled [[context-window-512-tokens|512-token context window]], not a short padded fragment.

One update therefore covers $64 \times 512 = 32{,}768$ token positions. [[language-modeling-objective|The objective]] contributes one term per position, so each gradient is an average over 32,768 next-token predictions.

Run the same arithmetic on warmup: 2000 updates times 64 sequences is 128,000 sequences, or roughly 65 million predicted tokens, passing through the model before the step size reaches full size.

Sampling contiguous spans rather than shuffled sentences is where the corpus choice cashes out. A 512-token window only buys long-range conditioning if the 512 tokens genuinely follow one another.

Three regularizers run alongside all of this — dropout in three places, and a weight decay adapted for Adam. They are set out in [[regularization-setup|the regularization setup]], and they, rather than the schedule, are where the run's defence against overfitting sits.

### How strong the evidence is

Thin, in the way that matters: none of these choices is ablated. The paper reports [[token-level-perplexity|a token-level perplexity of 18.4]] on the corpus, which says the run fit the data. It does not say a different schedule would have fit it worse.

The right panel of [[fig-2]] shows zero-shot task scores rising steadily across pre-training rather than stalling or collapsing, which is consistent with a stable run. It was built to argue something else, though, and is not a hyperparameter check.

The one further signal is indirect and arrives later in the paper: [[fine-tuning-lr-and-batch|fine-tuning reuses these settings]], changing only the peak learning rate — about four times smaller — the batch size, and the epoch count. The pre-training recipe was good enough to keep as the default.

This is the settings list for stage two: the actual optimizer configuration used when [[supervised-fine-tuning|the pre-trained stack is adapted to a labelled task]]. It is here because the paper's argument is not only that transfer works but that it is cheap, and a hyperparameter list is where "cheap" becomes checkable.

The stated default is inheritance. Unless the paper names an exception, fine-tuning keeps whatever [[pre-training-optimization|stage one used]] — Adam, the [[decoupled-weight-decay]] at $w = 0.01$, the residual, embedding and attention dropouts at 0.1, the same vocabulary, the same 512-token window. Nothing is frozen and nothing is re-initialized except the task head.

Four things change. A fresh dropout goes on the classifier ([[classifier-dropout]]); the optimization settings drop to [[fine-tuning-lr-and-batch|6.25e-5 with batches of 32]]; the run lasts [[three-epochs-fine-tuning|three epochs]]; and the schedule becomes [[fine-tuning-lr-schedule|linear decay after a 0.2% warmup]]. The auxiliary language modelling term is carried alongside the task loss at [[auxiliary-objective-weight|$\lambda = 0.5$]].

### Warmup as a fraction, not a count

Pre-training warmed up over a fixed 2000 updates. Fine-tuning instead warms up over 0.2% of whatever the run turns out to be, which makes the same line of configuration mean different things on different datasets.

Walk it. [[snli|SNLI]] has roughly 550k training examples, so three epochs at batch 32 is about $550{,}000 \times 3 / 32 \approx 51{,}500$ updates, and 0.2% of that is around 100 warmup steps. [[rte|RTE]] has 2490 examples, giving about 233 updates in total, so its warmup is well under a single step.

On the small datasets, then, the warmup is decoration. One expression covers twelve datasets without per-task tuning, and that uniformity is the point.

### What the numbers rest on

The contrast the paper wants is with methods like [[ulmfit|ULMFiT]], which adapts a pre-trained LSTM through a staged schedule of unfreezing and per-layer rates. Here every layer moves at one rate for three passes. The paper groups staged schemes with the intricacy it is trying to avoid.

The evidence is indirect. No ablation varies the learning rate, the epoch count or the warmup fraction; [[table-5]] ablates the auxiliary objective, the architecture and pre-training itself, not these settings. Support for "3 epochs was sufficient" is just that the reported [[evaluation-task-families|benchmark numbers]] were produced under it.

And the hedges are doing work. "For most tasks" and "for most cases" concede that some runs used something else, and the paper does not say which tasks deviated or what they used instead.

This is the paper's evaluation menu: the fixed list of supervised tasks the single pre-trained model is asked to do. It exists because the claim being tested is breadth — that one set of weights, adapted cheaply, competes with systems built one per task — and breadth can only be shown by measuring on many tasks at once.

### What varies across the twelve runs, and what does not

The twelve datasets are grouped into four families, laid out in [[table-1]]. [[natural-language-inference|Natural language inference]] takes five of them, [[question-answering-and-commonsense-reasoning|question answering and commonsense reasoning]] two, [[semantic-similarity]] three, and [[text-classification]] two. Five plus two plus three plus two is twelve. Several are pulled from the [[glue-benchmark|GLUE]] bundle, which is why an aggregate GLUE score can also be reported.

Each dataset gets its own fine-tuning run, so there are twelve fine-tuned models, not one. But they all start from the same pre-trained weights, and what differs between runs is small: the [[task-specific-input-transformations|input transformation]] that flattens a premise-hypothesis pair or a document-question-answer triplet into one token sequence, and the [[linear-output-layer-wy|linear output layer]] sized to that task's label set. The stack itself is untouched, which is what [[supervised-fine-tuning]] describes.

### What the spread buys and what it costs

The datasets differ by about two orders of magnitude in size, from roughly 5.7k training examples on [[sts-b|STS-B]] to roughly 550k on [[snli|SNLI]]. The paper uses that range to head off the obvious objection that pre-training only pays on tasks that already have plenty of labels.

The headline is [[state-of-the-art-9-of-12|nine of twelve]]. The three that are not beaten are informative: [[rte|RTE]], where 56% falls short of 61.7% from a multi-task biLSTM, [[sst-2|SST-2]] at 91.3%, described as competitive rather than better, and [[mrpc|MRPC]]. The paper offers a guess for RTE — that its model would likely also benefit from multi-task training — and says plainly it did not try.

Read the numbers with some care. Each is a single run against a single previously published best, with no variance reported and no shared training budget across the [[baseline-comparisons|baselines]], some of which are ensembles and some single models. Gains are stated as [[absolute-improvement|percentage-point differences]], which flatters a task with a low ceiling and understates one near saturation. What the table supports well is that the recipe does not collapse on any family of [[natural-language-understanding|language understanding]] task tried; the per-dataset margins carry less weight than the count.

Fine-tuning does not have to start from the whole pre-trained network. This analysis turns the amount transferred into a dial, and measures what each turn of it buys.

The dial has thirteen settings. At zero, nothing but the embeddings comes across from pre-training: the token table $W_e$ and the position table $W_p$ that together form the layer-zero input [[input-representation-h0|$h_0$]]. At twelve, every block of the stack comes across as well, which is the ordinary [[supervised-fine-tuning|fine-tuning]] setup. The settings in between carry the bottom $k$ blocks and leave the remaining $12-k$ to be initialized fresh, though the paper does not spell that detail out. The sweep only has this many settings because the model is [[twelve-layer-depth|twelve blocks deep]]; a shallower stack would give a shorter curve and less room for a trend to appear.

Each setting is then fine-tuned normally and scored on the development sets of [[multinli|MultiNLI]] and [[race-dataset|RACE]].

### What the curve shows

The result is the left panel of [[fig-2]]. Accuracy rises with $k$ rather than flattening after the first block or two, and the gap between zero layers and full transfer reaches about 9% on MultiNLI.

The first part of that is the expected part. Carrying a pre-trained embedding table into a supervised model is [[word-embedding-transfer|long-standing practice]], and the paper calls the gain from it the standard result.

The rest is the argument. If most of the transferable content lived in the embeddings, the curve would climb early and then level off. It does not, so the paper reads each layer as containing useful functionality for the target task.

### How much this carries

The claim is stated carefully in the paper, and it is worth keeping it that careful. What is measured is end accuracy at each setting, not what any individual layer holds; "useful functionality" is an inference from the shape of a curve, not something the experiment isolates.

The evidence is also thin in the ordinary ways. It is one figure, two datasets, development accuracy, and no reported repeats or variance across seeds. The 9% is the best case at the best setting on one of the two tasks, not a typical figure — RACE gains less.

Read against the [[ablation-no-pretraining|no-pre-training ablation]], which costs 14.8% on average, the ranking is consistent: pre-training matters most, and depth of transfer accounts for a substantial share of it.

The paper wants an explanation, not only a scoreboard: why does [[generative-pretraining|generative pre-training]] of a transformer transfer so well? Its stated hypothesis is that the generative model learns to do many of the evaluation tasks in the course of getting better at predicting the next token, and this analysis is the attempt to look at that directly.

The test removes the supervised half of the recipe. There is no [[supervised-fine-tuning|fine-tuning]], no trained classifier head and no labelled data — the pre-trained model has to produce answers as it stands.

### Turning the model into a scorer

That is not free, because a language model does not emit labels. It emits a distribution over the vocabulary at each position. So each task needs a hand-written rule that converts *what probability do you assign this string* into *which option do you pick*.

Three of the four rules use the same device, [[average-token-log-probability-scoring|average token log-probability]]. Take a candidate string of $m$ tokens. Sum the log-probabilities the model gives those tokens, under the same likelihood [[eq-lm-objective|$L_1$]] it was trained on. Divide by $m$.

The division is doing work. Every extra token adds a negative number, so a raw sum systematically favours the shortest candidate. The mean takes that length effect out, which matters when the options are answers of different lengths.

From there the four settings differ. [[cola-zero-shot-heuristic|CoLA]] thresholds the score of a single sentence. [[race-zero-shot-heuristic|RACE]] takes the highest-scoring answer given the document and question. [[dprd-winograd-heuristic|DPRD]] compares the two pronoun substitutions. [[sst2-zero-shot-heuristic|SST-2]] is the one that does not use a mean at all, and instead reads off a restricted two-word output distribution.

### What the curves support

Each heuristic is then run at checkpoints across pre-training and plotted against updates, in the right panel of [[fig-2]]. The reported pattern is that the scores are stable and rise steadily. The paper reads that as pre-training supporting task-relevant functionality, rather than fine-tuning building it — the same direction as [[layers-transferred|the layer-transfer curve]] on the left.

The same heuristics were run on an [[lstm-gpt1|LSTM]] trained in the same framework, which the paper says shows higher variance across pre-training. That single observation is the whole support for [[transformer-inductive-bias]], and the paper words it as a suggestion.

Be clear about the strength. The heuristics are the authors' own inventions, so an absolute number says as much about the rule as about the model, and the curves are trends rather than competitive task scores. There are four settings, one of them (DPRD) outside the twelve evaluation datasets. "Higher variance" is read off a plot with no interval attached. This diagnostic carries less weight than the [[ablation-studies|ablation]] numbers.

The benchmark tables show the full recipe winning. [[table-5]] is the paper's attempt to find out which parts of the recipe are responsible, by building three cut-down versions of the system and running each one through the same evaluation.

Every ablation is a separate end-to-end training run. One piece is removed or replaced, everything else — the serialized inputs, the last-token readout, the fine-tuning schedule — is held fixed, and the resulting scores are compared against the full model on an unweighted average across the tasks in the table.

The first removal deletes stage one. [[ablation-no-pretraining|Skipping pre-training]] keeps the same 12-layer decoder and trains it straight on each labelled dataset, so the weights it starts from are random rather than inherited from [[generative-pretraining|generative pre-training]]. That costs 14.8%, and the paper reports it hurting on every task, not just on average.

The second removal keeps the two stages and changes the sequence model. [[ablation-lstm-substitution|Substituting an LSTM]] puts a single-layer, 2048-unit recurrent net where the [[multi-layer-transformer-decoder|transformer decoder]] was. The average falls by 5.6 points, and [[mrpc|MRPC]] is the one dataset where the LSTM comes out ahead.

The third removal touches only the loss. [[ablation-no-auxiliary-objective|Dropping the auxiliary objective]] switches off the $\lambda L_1$ term that [[auxiliary-lm-objective|keeps language modelling alive during fine-tuning]], leaving the label loss alone in [[supervised-fine-tuning|stage two]]. Removing it gains 0.3 on average. It helps on [[qqp]] and the NLI sets and hurts on the smaller ones, which the paper reads as a size-dependent effect.

Put the three numbers side by side and an ordering falls out. 14.8 against 5.6 is roughly three to one, so on this evidence the pre-training matters about three times as much as the architecture choice it runs on. The third effect is not even reliably positive; the aggregate mildly favours removing the term the paper chose to keep.

### How much weight the numbers carry

Each row is one training run at one setting. There are no seeds, no error bars, and no sweep behind them, so a few points of average score is a soft measurement.

The architecture comparison is the loosest of the three. A single-layer 2048-unit LSTM differs from a twelve-layer transformer in depth and parameter count as well as in recurrence, so 5.6 points is not cleanly attributable to attention alone.

The auxiliary result is confounded in a different way: [[auxiliary-objective-weight|$\lambda$ is fixed at 0.5]] everywhere, so a term whose sign of effect tracks dataset size is being applied at one strength across all of them.

The no-pre-training row is the cleanest and the largest, and it is the number the rest of the paper leans on.

GPT-1 trains a single transformer decoder to predict the next token over 7,000-plus unpublished books, then keeps those weights and fine-tunes them, with one linear layer on top, on twelve labelled datasets. Most of the machinery inside that network was defined in other papers; what this paper puts forward is the [[two-stage-training-procedure]] and the input rewrites that let one unchanged architecture cover four task families.

### What it takes from papers already here

The backbone is the architecture of [[transformer]], adopted more or less wholesale: Section 4.1 says the model "largely follows the original transformer work" and then records only the deltas. What GPT-1 keeps is the [[decoder-stack]]'s pair of sublayers — masked multi-head self-attention, then a position-wise feed-forward network — and what it drops is [[encoder-decoder-attention]], because there is no encoder for it to read. That cut is not described in GPT-1 either; Section 3.1 cites [34] for it, where deleting the encoder module and leaving one stack is set out as [[transformer-decoder-t-d]]. The motivation there is [[transduction-as-single-sequence-lm]]: concatenate source and target into one stream with a separator and train a plain language model on it. GPT-1 takes the shape and not the motivation. Its stream is contiguous book text, and its [[model-specification]] fills the shape in at 12 layers, 768-dimensional states, 12 heads and 3072-dimensional feed-forward inner states.

Tokenization is a merge count and nothing more. GPT-1 says it used "a bytepair encoding (BPE) vocabulary with 40,000 merges" and moves on. The greedy loop that produces those merges is [[bpe-merge-algorithm]], and the reason a merge count is a sufficient specification is [[bpe-vocabulary-size]]: the final symbol vocabulary is the initial character vocabulary plus the number of merges, and that count is the algorithm's only knob. The unit matters for reading GPT-1's numbers — the token-level [[perplexity]] of 18.4 on BooksCorpus is measured in 40,000-merge subwords, not words.

Three more pieces are named and left undefined. GPT-1 uses GELU at the 3072-dimensional point of every feed-forward sublayer without writing the formula down; [[gelu-definition]] gives it as $x \cdot \Phi(x)$, [[gelu-tanh-approximation]] gives the cheap substitute most implementations actually run, and [[gelu-vs-relu-and-elu]] is where it is placed against the [[relu]] the original transformer used. The optimizer line is similar: "a modified version of L2 regularization proposed in [37], with $w = 0.01$ on all non bias or gain weights". What the modification is, and why an adaptive step size makes L2 and weight decay come apart, is [[adaptive-preconditioner-dilutes-l2]]; the resulting update is [[decoupled-weight-decay-update]]. And the serialization that makes [[task-specific-input-transformations]] possible — premise, delimiter, hypothesis, read as one left-to-right stream — is [[conditional-encoding]], with the separator token itself as [[premise-hypothesis-delimiter]] and the read-off-the-last-vector classifier as [[last-output-vector-classifier]]. That paper's own reader is an LSTM; GPT-1 borrows the serialization, not the architecture.

Layer normalization is the odd one. GPT-1 mentions it once, as a justification rather than a component: "since layernorm [2] is used extensively throughout the model, a simple weight initialization of $N(0, 0.02)$ was sufficient". The scheme itself is [[layer-normalization-statistics]], and the closest thing to a reason for that inference is [[normalization-invariance-properties]] — the network's output is invariant to rescaling a whole weight matrix. But neither paper runs the initialization experiment. GPT-1 asserts sufficiency in one clause and reports no sweep over it.

Some of what GPT-1 leans on has no paper here at all. Adam is cited to Kingma & Ba, which is not in this project; [[adam-optimizer]] appears only as a one-line description in the transformer paper, so the update rule behind GPT-1's 2.5e-4 cosine schedule is not covered. Nor is the semi-supervised line the paper places itself in — ELMo, ULMFiT, Dai and Le, pre-trained word vectors — or any of the twelve evaluation datasets.

### Where it diverges, and where it goes elsewhere

Against [[encoder-decoder-architecture]] the difference is not a tweak. That design exists to do [[sequence-transduction]]: an encoder reads a source sequence with unmasked attention, and a decoder generates a target while attending back into it. GPT-1 has no source sequence. It has one stack with [[masked-self-attention]] at every layer, trained to continue text, and then bent to twelve tasks whose output is a label from a linear layer. The consequence is the whole of Section 3.3. With no encoder to hand structure to, anything a task needs — a premise and a hypothesis, a document and a question and four candidate answers — has to be flattened into the one stream the pre-trained model can read.

Positions diverge in the other direction, and this one is a swap rather than a cut. The original scheme is [[sinusoidal-positional-encoding]], fixed rather than trained, and that paper gives a reason for the fixed form: it may let the model extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than those seen in training. GPT-1 uses [[learned-position-embeddings]] instead — the [[learned-positional-embedding]] alternative the transformer paper reports as producing nearly identical translation results. The consequence is a table with one row per position, sized to GPT-1's 512-token training spans, learned from the pre-training corpus like any other parameter.

The evidence differs too, and so does what counts as success. The transformer is scored in [[bleu]] on [[wmt-2014-en-de]] and [[wmt-2014-en-fr]], with [[constituency-parsing]] as its one test outside translation — still a sequence generated from a sequence. GPT-1 reports accuracy and correlation across [[evaluation-task-families]]: entailment, question answering and commonsense reasoning, semantic similarity, and classification. Neither set of numbers can be read against the other. Even the training data is chosen for a different property: GPT-1 takes contiguous 512-token spans from books over the same-sized 1B Word Benchmark precisely because sentence-level shuffling destroys the long-range structure it wants to condition on.

### What this does not establish

None of these papers were run against each other. No shared model, corpus, or metric connects them, and nothing here is an ablation: removing GELU or learned positions from GPT-1 was not tested, so their contribution to its results is not measured by anything on this page. Reading a mechanism in the paper that defines it tells you what GPT-1 turned on, and at which setting. It does not tell you how much that setting bought.
